speechtext:
Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (for the Minister of Finance) moved the second reading
of Bill No. 74, to levy a Tax on Business Profits.

Mr. Speaker, by arrangement with the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), it was understood that on the second reading of this Bill, we would be at liberty to discuss in a general way its provisions, also the provisions of the tariff amendments under Bill No. 16 that had its second reading last week, and also any matters relating generally to expenditures. Accordingly, I take advantage of the opportunity to occupy the attention of the House for a few moments upon these matters. In the first place, in connection with the Bill now before the House, I beg to call the' attention of the Minister of Finance to the title. Section 1 reads as followis:
This Act may be cited as the business profits tax Act, 1916.
It was stated by the minister in his Budget speech, and frequently afterwards, that this taxation measure was to continue in force but for a period of two years, and that it was in essence a war measure. I therefore beg to suggest that the title of the Bill should be amended so that it may be cited as the " Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916," and not as it now reads. I think that with that amendment it will be made clearer to the country that the Bill is intended as a war measure purely and that the revenues to be derived under its provisions are for war purposes. I suggest this amendment also because it will be a further assurance to the country that the Bill goes into operation as but a temporary expedient for the raising of revenue for war purposes.
When speaking upon the Budget I expressed my opinion in reference to the principle involved in this Bill and I do not intend to occupy the time of the House in reiterating my views. I then stated what were, in my opinion, the fundamental objections to the Bill, and while they have been somewhat amended, my objections in substance still remain. My criticism of the taxation of business profits is that it eliminates as contributors to war revenues a great number of people who, I believe are willing to contribute, and who should be contributing at this time. There are a large number of people in this country in receipt of very substantial incomes from accumulated wealth of one kind and another, and it does seem an invidious distinction that in this period of financial stress, they should be eliminated as contributors to the public

revenues for war purposes. That is an objection to the revenue measure of the Minister of Finance that is fundamentally sound and one which cannot well be answered by him. It is all very well to say that this Bill applies to a particular class only, and was only intended to apply to that class, but I do say it is objectionable to find a large number of people in the country to whom this measure will riot apply when they are financially competent Ito respond very handsomely, and I think in many cases are quite willing to be taxed for such purposes. While business in this country to-day is quite prosperous, while the very men engaged in business are making handsome profits, still it is nevertheless the fact that in the period immediately preceding the cessation of war, and for some times afterwards, there will be disastrous declines in business and many will suffer very heavily. They might very well argue that they should be allowed to keep as large a proportion of war time profits in their possession as possible in order to meet the losses which inevitably will come upon them in the -months immediately preceding the arrangements for peace and for months, possibly years, following peace.
Having said these, few words in reference to the business profits taxation features of the Bill, I wish to say just a few words in relation to the mining taxation. After having given some reflection to the proposals to tax mining profits since the introduction of the measure to the House, I am still Of the opinion that it is a mistake and not in the interest of the country. We wish increased production of natural resources. Increased production of natural resources at the present time, and for years to come, will be out only method of paying off unfavourable trade balances and -heavy interest accounts abroad. There is, furthermore, this very serious objection: it will prevent the inflow of foreign capital for investment in the mining industry, particularly as regards metalliferous mines. It may be that the tax of 25 per cent on profits over 7 per cent may sound more dangerous than it really is, but the fact remains that up to the present time, some hundreds of thousands of dollars which would have come to Canada for investment in the mining industry have been withheld; that will be true of the future. But if the minister will persist in this taxation of mining profits, the percentage beyond which profits are taxed should be increased beyond 7 to 10
TMr. A. K. Maclean.]
per cent, for it is generally agreed that the industry is entitled to very much larger profits than that. I do not think it is fair to the mining industry to exempt profits only up to 7 of 10 per cent. The minister and his department are taking authority to issue regulations providing for a just method of arriving at the amount that should be deducted for the exhaustion of ore bodies. That is a very difficult thing to work out, and 1 'oubt whether it pan be done successfully. On the whole, then, this taxation, so far as the mining industry is concerned, is an unfortunate thing; it will impede investment of foreign capital, and prevent the development of that source of national wealth and, as a consequence, affect our revenue; and therefore I say that the Minister of Finance will not obtain from this tax on the mines industry any substantial amount of revenue. On the other hand, it, will deal what I fear will be a disastrous blow to a very important industry in this country. For these reasons I think this tax should be abandoned, or at least substantially amended.
Just a word with reference to the taxation of industries engaged in the supply of war munitions. In my remarks upon the Budget, I said I thonght it would be better business to see that all war supplies and munitions purchased by the Government should be supplied at a fair price.. I reaffirm that position to-day. But, if we are to tax profits made by those who are supplying munitions of war to the Government of this country, I think we are fairly entitled to receive from that source a greater percentage than the 25 per cent which the Bill provides for. I do not think that proposition can very well be controverted. In my opinion this class should be made to contribute more than 25 per cent of their profits in excess of ithe stipulated 7 per cent.
I was absent from the House when the Customs Tariff Bill was passed last week, and I should like to say just a few words upon it now. It seems to me a reprehensible thing, at this particular time, to increase, for protective purposes, the tariff upon any one particular product. I should have thought the abilities of the Minister of Finance would have been amply taxed in securing sufficient revenues for this country, without devoting any of his time to tariff amendments made purely for protective purposes and which will consequently cut down our revenues. However

strongly one might believe in a protective policy for this country, one hardly expects to find anyone bold enough to contend that m view of existing conditions, that there was any necessity whatever for increasing at the present time the tariff upon any one particular article for protective purposes. When you consider the great demand there is to-day for practically-everything we produce in this country, and the disabilities which importers and consumers suffer by reason of the lack of shipping, the high rates of insurance, one would think that these conditions alone afforded sufficient protection for any industry in this country, regardless of the tariff. I therefore say that it is reprenhensible that the minister should have seen fit at this time to increase the tariff on apples, and impose taxation for protective purposes upon fuel oil. The duty on apples will not accomplish the result the minister expects, and it will lay an increased burden on certain consumers i,n this country at a time when they should not (be expected to bear it In respect to the tariff rates to be imposed upon fuel oil, the Government has not given Parliament good and sufficient reasons for its imposition. The lack of shipping facilities for bringing oil from the United States to British Columbia should alone have been a sufficient protection for coal, if that was the purpose of this tax. I therefore submit that the House has not been given reasons sufficient to justify the two changes that have been made in the Customs Tariff Bill which passed * the House last week. There is no necessity at the present time for the imposition of any duty for protective purposes-and it was' admitted that these tariff changes were made for that purpose. The consumers in this country can not well afford to bear this additional taxation at the present time.
With regard to the tariff imposition of last year, and particularly the surtax of 7\ per cent upon the general tariff, I would point out that that tax has been in force now for practically a year, and I think it is quite clear that as a revenue measure it has been a failure. It is quite true that the minister secured a very substantial .additional revenue from his tariff taxation Bill of last year but it came from the 7i per cent tax upon free goods. That is a tariff imposed for revenue purposes, it is probably not so objectionable although it has been indiscriminately applied. I want to repeat what I
said a moment ago that, from the revenue standpoint, the surtax of 7i per cent imposed on the general tariff last year was a failure, apd should be removed. Our general tariff is at any time a very high one, and if we take into consideration the disabilities which the importer and the consumer encounter in the lack of transportation, in the high cost of insurance and in the high interest rates, surely they afford more than sufficient additional protection without our imposing the additional tax of 7i per cent. The 7J per cent added to the general, tariff is virtually prohibition against importation of a great many commodities; it imposes a burden which the people of this country should not be asked to bear at the present moment, and it should 'be removed.

Has there been any general complaint or condemnation of the 71 per cent?
Mr. MACLEAN; I think the complaint is general and unqualified. When the Minister of Finance last year introduced his tariff measure providing for the surtax of 7i per cent to the igenefal tariff he assured the country that the manufacturers would not add this tariff to the cost of their productions. In fact, I think my hon. friend the member for Peel deliberately gave us in this House his personal assurance that this tax would not add to the cost of commodities.
My hon. friend is wrong in that, but it is unimportant.

I do not think I am wrong, because I think one of my colleagues upon this side of the House, on the occasion of that statement being made by my hon. friend, read to the House a trade circular issued from Peel county disclaiming any intention on the part of a manufacturer to impose the additional 7i per cent to the cost of goods.
I was asking my hon, friend if there had been any special protest to the House of Commons or to the Government complaining against the 7t per cent to which my hon. friend is referring.

I am not in a position to know what protests the Minister of Finance has received from the Canadian people, but I have no doubt he has received hundreds of protests. We, however, as the representatives of the people are here to protest against any unfair tax being im-
If the people are living under a delusion, how does it come about that there are complaints?

No complaints? My
hon. friend is wrong in saying that there are no complaints. -
Where is the delusion?
It is a notorious fact. I am saying that the delusion is harboured toy hon. gentlemen like my friend.
I beg your pardon.

He is under the delusion that this ^country is living in a period of such prosperity that no one is suffering from the high-pri'ced commodities which are of daily domestic use. For this reason, therefore, Parliament should take into consideration the question of the elimination of the surtax of 7j per cent, first, because it gives us no substantial additional revenue, and, secondly, because it operates as an unnatural degree of protection, and works out as practically a prohibition against importation, and consequently con-

tributes to the making of high prices of products.
We require additional revenue in this country, and ,we upon this side of the House, realizing that fact, do not Object to any efforts made by the Government in order to secure that additional revenue. Our interest account is climbing. Very shortly we shall be obliged to meet a very heavy pension list. There will be a diminution in excise revenue from liquors because of the general adoption of prohibitory measures by the several provinces. Therefore, for these and other causes, it is desirable that our revenue should be increased. There are some hon. gentlemen who consider it is not good business to impose additional taxation upon the people of a country in a time of war. Personally, I do not agree with that view. As I have pointed out on more than one occasion in the past, there are two ways of securing revenue: first, toy the imposition of fresh taxation measures, and, secondly, by measures of internal economy and the abandonment of expenditures that can be postponed, or that can be done away with entirely. These are the only two methods of meeting the financial necessities of the country to-day.
We upon this side of the House have frequently endeavoured to impress upon the Government the great necessity of economy in expenditure. We have urged this in the House and in Committee of Supply on many occasions, but I doubt very much if we have succeeded in impressing the members of the. Government as much as we hoped to do, or as we believe ,the country would like them to be impressed. The people will not object to taxation provided that it is used for the purposes for which it is imposed; but they will object to any taxation measures to produce revenue if a saving corresponding to the amount of such taxation might have been made in our ordinary expenditures which would have obviated the necessity for this taxation. There is- no purpose in securing twenty-five or thirty million dollars of revenue by fresh taxation if an equal amount by careful, economical administration might be saved in our general expenditures.
I think that that is a statement which can scarcely be gainsaid, and I am glad to see the hon. member for West Peterborough concur in it.
Two and two make four.

It is our duty as representatives-particularly is it the duty of

hon. gentlemen on this side of the House- to continue to press upon the Government the great necessity and importance of reducing expenditure to the lowest possible amount.
The member for Edmonton (Hon. Frank Oliver) the other night read a statement recently made by the Prime Minister of Great Britain which I should like again to read, because some of the members present to-day may not have heard the member for Edmonton give that statement to the House. The statement of the Prime Minister of Great Britain, which refers to expenditure, was as follows:
In view of the stupendous and unprecedented liabilities and obligations which the war is imposing upon us, if we are, as I think we are still agreed that we are to subordinate every other purpose to its effectual and successful prosecution, one of the first means which prudence and policy prescribe in the attainment of that object is the temporary reduction in every form, both of public and of private expenditure, which can be shown not to be directly conductive to that purpose.
Hon. gentlemen opposite, in answer to my contentions, will say: we have reduced very considerably the expenditures in this and that department-and they will point to very substantial reductions in what we call the larger expenditures. But the Government cannot effect the necessary reduction in public expenditure unless they recognise the value of reduction in the expenditures in connection with smaller matters; unless they go into the expenditures of the various departments in detail and endeavour to save here and there this and that amount, be it small or large. It is not sufficient for the Government to postpone the expenditure of amounts of money which involve millions of dollars, because the millions are, after all, composed of thousands, and if they can save the thousands they can effect a saving of millions.
We have discussed the expenditures of several departments here on many occasions; I wish very briefly to address myself to the House on that subject. We have frequently referred to the expenditures of the Public Works Department. True, there has been a reduction in that department. In the fiscal year ending March 31 last there was a very substantial reduction in expenditure over that of the previous fiscal year. But this reduction, after all, was not sufficient. I was surprised when I saw the character of some of the expenditures made up to December 31 last. I could understand that for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1915, we would have some large expenditures which had been commenced before the beginning of the war and which it was necessary for the Government to proceed with, but for the year ending March 31 last there were many expenditures upon public works which might well have been postponed. The expenditures of that department for 1911-12, as has been frequently pointed out, amounted in round figures to $10,000,000; they amount to over $12,000,000 for the year which has just ended. Will any man say that the Public Works Department could not have conducted its affairs during the past year with $10,000,000 as well as it could in 1911-12 under much more favourable conditions? Had they done this it would have effected a saving of $2,000,000, one-quarter of the amount which the Minister of Finance will get out of the operation of the Bill which is now before us, I assume that he contemplates a total revenue from the business profits tax of between $25,000,000 and $30,000,000 in the three years, or an annual revenue of about. $8,000,000. The Minister of Public Works and all members of the Government say that they do not purpose expending all the amounts set forth in the Estimates. Here let me say that when the Government take the position that they are justified in asking Parliament to vote sums of money which they do not contemplate expending, they are assuming a position which is constitutionally wrong. Hon. gentlemen have read an address delivered by a member of the parliamentary press gallery at a political club in Montreal the other day in which he dealt with the idea that Parliament is abdicating its true functions. Unfortunately, there is a good deal of truth in that view. In this country we have not Government by Cabinet; it is for Parliament to determine what moneys shall be voted and the purposes for which those moneys shall be expended. It should not be left to the discretion of members of the Government to determine whether they shall or shall not spend certain moneys. If Parliament does not contemplate the expenditure of certain moneys, the items in reference to them should have no place in the Estimates, and constitutionally speaking the Government are taking a false position when they ask us to vote moneys which they do not purpose expending.
Let me take another illustration in order to point out that the Government are not properly seized of the necessity of a proper investigation of the smaller expenditures

with a view to reduction and the curtailment of the total expenditure. In 1911-12 civil government cost the country $4,774,000; in 1914-15, $6,157,000, and we are asked to vote for next year $7,240,000, an increase of nearly 80 per cent in four years. The, fact that the .Estimates provide for a larger amount for the present fiscal year than was expended last year is an intimation that there is to be an increase in the Civil Service somewhere, either in numbers or by way of salaries. I think I may say without fear of successful contradiction that there cannot conceivably be anything to justify an increase in the cost of administration on account of civil government. There are many branches of the public service where the employees can have very little to do to-day. It is true that in one or two departments the number of employees has had to be increased. I assume that in the Militia Department a great number of clerks must have been added to the staffs since the beginning of the war. I can understand the necessity for that. I notice by a printed document which was distributed to the members of the House today that a great number of persons have been employed and are being employed by the War Purchasing Commission, numbering some 200. I suggest, and I think it is a fair suggestion, that the Government should have taken employees from these departments of the Government in which work has decreased and transferred them to those departments where additional work was created by the war. If 200 or 300 more people are employed by the Militia Department, if 200 persons are employed by the War Purchasing Commission, why could there not have been a transfer of civil servants from other branches to these particular departments, thus effecting a saving? The fact that civil government next year will likely cost over $7,000,000, as against something like $4,500,000 four and one-half years ago, is deserving of the investigation of Parliament and the consideration of the Government. I venture to say, even in a dogmatic fashion, that there can be no justification whatever for the whole of this increase. And we must remember that if in this way $1,000,000 could be saved, that would provide one-eighth of the total amount which the minister expects to receive from the Bill we are now considering. I say it is better to get a million dollars of revenue in that way than by taking it from the pockets of the people, and I know rMr. A. K. Maclean.]
that my hon. friend from Peterborough will agree with me.

Since my hon. friend
has referred to me, I think the statement that there is no justification for this increased expenditure certainly ought to be revised and ought not to go to the country.

I should not like to be understood as saying that there is no justification for any increase in any of the departments of the Government, but I repeat that I doufbt if there is any reason for that increase from $4,470,000 in 1912 to $7,240,000 in civil Government for the present year. It may he that my hon. friend may be able to justify some slight increase, but we will not occupy the time of Parliament this afternoon in discussing that. I was speaking in a general way.
Let us take the large expenditures in connection with immigration. This was discussed at length a few evenings ago, when the Minister of the Interior was in Supply. We find that the expenditures for 1914-15 were larger than ever before in the history o'f this country. The amounts which we are asked for the next fiscal year *are very substantial. Our im-
4 p.m. migration has fallen to a negligible quantity, and it is very doubtful indeed if we should even make any great effort at the present moment to secure immigration into this country. I think it is hardly fair to go to Great Britain and the European countries which are our Allies and there carry on an immigration propaganda.
Hear, hear.

Many things contribute to operate against a successful immigration campaign in the United States at the present moment. I do not say that we should abandon altogether our efforts to secure immigration, but I do say that we might very well pause and determine what will be our policy in respect to immigration before we again embark upon any vigorous policy in that regard. It is true, as has been said by some hon. gentlemen opposite, that the Immigration Branch has in its employ, in Europe, the United States, and elsewhere, a great number of officials who have been long engaged in this work, and that it would be unfair and unjust to deprive them of their employment. My answer to that is that their services could be transferred from that branch of the public service to another department of the service.

that other work could .be found for them to the advantage of the country. Closely related to immigration, there is the quarantine service, and while the expense in that connection is, relatively speaking, small, still it is quite a substantial amount. One would think that having no immigration or practically none, we would see some diminution in the cost of administering the quarantine branch, particularly at the eastern ports. During the last calendar year, there were landed at Halifax only 1,425 immigrants; at St. John, 1,697; at Quebec, 6,168; at Vancouver, 118; and at Victoria, 477; practically none. One would imagine that with this small immigration the expenditures of the quarantine branch might be very well reduced to a small amount. Surely the services of most of the medical men employed as quarantine officers at the several ports might be dispensed with. They are usually professional gentlemen who have private practices, and they could be very easily removed without causing any hardship. For instance, I find in the port of Halifax this condition, that there are there three medical men employed at yearly salaries of $1,200, $1,800 and $1,200 respectively. That is $4,200 altogether. During last year only 1,425 immigrants landed there. Two of these medical gentlemen have enlisted with pay. 1 do not see why medical gentlemen employed in the quarantine branch, if they enlist, should receive their salaries. I cannot understand that. It is surely unfair. They were only employed for a few months in the year at the most, and I say it is unfair to pay them their usual salaries. It is absolutely unfair, and there is no justification for it whatever. I find that one other medical officer has enlisted without pay. but another man has been appointed in his place. Among the quarantine officers at Quebec there are a great number of highly paid men and quite a number who are paid small amounts. They are employed for only a few months in the year. Some of them are medical gentlemen ' and have large practices, and I submit it is most objectionable that all these men should be continued in employment when there is practically no work for them to perform. These emjployees occupy quite a different position from the ordinary civil servant.
Do they receive both salaries?
Those who have enlisted? Apparently yes.
That is not the custom in the Civil Service.

I think it is true in that case. That is a relatively small matter, but a very great saving could be affected; it perhaps would amount to $100,000 anyway, and I say that that is worth saving. During the present and last session the Minister of Finance, in explaining his revenue taxation measures, stated that from this particular source, or that paritcular source, he expected to obtain $100,000 in revenue. I emphasize this point particularly for the purpose of pointing out to hon. gentlemen that a very great saving could be affected in our expenditures if some attention were paid to the smaller amounts. This is perhaps a small matter, but I refer to it more to illustrate the possibility of a total saving through various branches of the public service, if we lopped off $100,000 here, and $200,000 there, and a million dollars somewhere else.
Take the Indian Branch of the Department of the Interior. The amount there expended is quite substantial. In 1911-12 it was $1,756,000. In 1914, it had grown to $2,400,000, an increase of $700,000, without absolutely any justification whatever. I referred to this particular matter in discussing the Budget at the last session of Parliament. I think I gave to the House very cogent reasons why the Government, in increasing their expenditures in respect to this department, were open to censure, and I venture to say that I was not successfully answered. The expenditures for this branch for 1916-17 are estimated to amount to $1,965,000. There is no reason in the world why at the present moment, in connection with the Indian expenditures, we should not get back to the expenditures of 1910 and 1911. We would affect thereby a very considerable saving. There has been a very notable increase in my own province in connection with this branch.' The year before last a man was appointed as inspector who was not needed. The man who was then inspector had not enough to do, and did not want an assistant, and the Government could not even tell us who was responsible for the appointment. The Minister of the Interior threw the burden upon the Prime Minister and the Prime Minister disclaimed any knowledge; and the result was that not a single member of the Government would assume responsibility for this appointment. I venture to say that the person thus appointed as

inspector has not performed twenty-four hours' real service since his appointment. There is no reason why he should be retained; there was no reason why he should have been appointed. In my own province there are scores of doctors employed by the Interior Department as medical attendants for the Indians who cannot perform .any real service, and who were never expected to do so. Even if we cannot agree upon the desirability of dismissing them entirely and abolishing the office, surely hon. gentlemen opposite will agree with me that for the moment we should temporarily dispense with the services of most of them, *and thus effect a very considerable saving in this particular service.
Let me repeat that, in the Indian branch of the Department of the Interior, we could effect reductions in expenditures which would equal one-ninth or one-tenth of the total amount which the minister estimates to recover from the tax upon business profits. .

I heard the hon. gentleman say that two medical officers employed by the Government in the city of Halifax had enlisted, and that they were receiving double pay. I wish to make the statement that that is incorrect. A moment ago I telephones to the Immigration Commissioner, and he says they do not receive double pay.
Why ask the commissioner? You might as well ask my hon.' friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte.)
He is in control.
He has nothing to do with it at all.
I make the statement on the authority of the commissioner, and I am quite sure he is correct.

Early in the session I moved for a return showing the employees of the Government who had enlisted, and who were drawing double salary, and if that return had bean placed on the Table it might not have been necessary to speculate about whether they are receiving double pay or not.
There would be no need for speculation if my hon. friend would try to get at the facts.
Why is the information not on the Table?

I have no desire whatever to misrepresent the facts. I spoke from information afforded to me in a return for which I moved, and which I received just a few days .ago. I find that Edgar Douglas was appointed Immigration medical officer at Halifax on December 1, 1911, at a salary of $1,200, and under the heading, " When service ceased," I find " enlisted with pay." I find the same in respect to Dr. F. A. R. Gow, " enlisted with pay."

When did they enlist?
.Mr. MACLEAN: A few months ago, six months ago. Then I find that another medical officer, John Rankin, was appointed December 15, 1913, at a salary of $1,200, " enlisted without pay." But I find that after he enlisted without pay, another person was appointed on January 3, 1916, at $1,200 as a substitute for Dr. Rankin. Surely my bon. friend did not expect that medical officers should enlist and draw their pay, and still get a paid substitute in their .place.

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but as I understand it, there is no department in the Government that 'is now paying salary to men who have enlisted and who are drawing militia pay as well.
That is not correct.
I think it is correct; I think there is no doubt about it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend should blame the Government for giving a false return.

I am going to place myself in the strong position of relying on this return.
IMr. BLAIN: It is an old return; there has been a change since.
(Mr. MACLEAN: This return was presented to me just a few days ago.- If there has been any change recently, well and good.
Mr. BiLAEN: As I understand it, the change took place last November. Prior to last November, double salary was paid in many cases, perhaps in all cases; but my information is, and I am speaking in the hearing of ministers of the Crown, that since last November, no employee has received double pay. ,
That is right.
I said a moment ago that I preferred to take the statement furnished to me by the Government's return to the House in answer to a motion of mine.

I would expect my hon. friend to be up to date.
IMr. ROGERS: There is nothing in the return to show that they were getting double pay.
Just the other day the Minister of Justice stated that the inspector of penitentiaries at Kingston was getting his salary as inspector, and also his salary as a militia officer.

That is Inspector
Hughes?
That was before the change made in November.
He receives double pay anyway.

At any rate it is quite clear that the immigration officers at several ports in Eastern Canada have for some time at least received departmental- salaries, though practically without departmental employment. But supposing the position taken by my hon. friend from Peel is correct, and that it has been correct for some months past, I say that the fact that we had no immigration should have impelled the Government to revise their departmental policies in respect to employees at these ports where immigrants enter the country, and to reduce their staffs of immigrant medical officers, and abolish mainy offices, retaining just the number of men that were actually necessary.
Just a word or two about some of the other departments. In the Department of Marine and Fisheries I notice there has been steady and substantial increases in the expenditures. I have not recently investigated them in detail, and I will not say that some of them are not justified, but when I find that the expenditures have , grown from $843,000 iin 1911-12 to $1,455,000 last year I ask myself the question: Is that great increase justified; is it necessary for the efficiency of the department? Mind you, Mfr. Speaker, this is exclusive of the expenditures made specially for the Naval Service Branch. When hon. gentlemen opposite were sitting on this side I remember that frequently they occupied the time of the House in condemning the employment of so great a number of fishery officers in the several provinces. We were told that in my province there were hundreds of officers who were actually performing mo .service, and that their connection with the department should cease. There is no particular energy being displayed in the administration of the Fisheries Department at the present moment that I know of. There has been no new programme inaugurated requiring the labours of additional employees. Would not this be a good time for hon. gentlemen opposite to carry out some of the suggestions which they made a few years ago? I think it is quite true that perhaps in each province they could very well dispense with the services of 100 or 200 officials, if not absolutely for all time to come, then temporarily. We upon this side of the House feel that if during the period of the war we oan induce the Government to make any considerable saving in public expenditure we will have accomplished something, and we will feel that we have properly discharged our duties as an Opposition to the country. I venture to suggest to the Minister of Finance and the Government that if they will make a detailed investigation of the expenditures of that particular department, a saving of some hundreds of thousands of dollars might be made without doing any injury to the efficiency of the department or to any interest in the e >untry at large.
During the past week or more, or ever since the hon. Postmaster General made his statement, we have had more or less of a running discussion in connection with the expenditures of his department. I wish, however, to say a few words in addition to what has already been said by other hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. Let me give to the House the figures in respect to the expenditures, because I know figures rapidly, pass away from the minds of hon. gentlemen. Since this Government came into power the expenditures in the Post Office Department have been as follows:
1911-12	$ 9,172,000
1918-14	 12,956,000
1914-15	 15,950,000
1916-17 (estimated) . . ..	17,486,000
So that we have an increase of nearly $8,000,000 since 1911-12. That is a most startling increase. The obligation rests upon hon. gentlemen opposite to give very cogent reasons, much clearer reasons than they have given yet, for that tremendous increase in a period of five years. I do not deny the proposition that we must expect increases in some of the great departments of the public service. In many cases it is



a good indication, and in itself it affords no ground upon which one may condemn a Government or a department. But we have expected from the Postmaster General some more valid reason for this great increase than we have received from that hon. gentleman up to the present time. What I fear is that hon. gentlemen opposite are reverting to their natural tendency to deficits in that particular branch of the service. Hon. gentlemen opposite have a record behind them in respect to this department. I find that during the period when they were in power, prior to 1890, it usually cost this country 30 per cent more than the total revenue to administer the department. I find that some time after the late Administration came into office, from 1901 or 1902 down, that department was administered at a cost of about 90 per cent of the total revenue, and that it had a surplus of about 10 per cent. Some hon. gentlemen opposite took the position a few days ago that this branch of the public service should not be able to boast a surplus, and that all the revenue from this source should always be expended for the advantage of the public. There is something to say in favour of that, but that is not the position in which we find ourselves. We do not find that the revenue has merely been expended, but we find a tremendous deficit. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) advanced that argument some two or three weeks ago, but if that were the position to-day the Opposition would not be upon such strong ground as that which we occupy. It is not a question of the Government not having a surplus, but it is a question of a deficit last year of $3,000,000, a deficit tips year of perhaps $5,000,000, and, if they keep on at the same ratio, a deficit next year of probably $6,000,000 or $7,000,000. I submit that it is a good business proposition that there should be some parity between income and outgo in connection with the administration of any branch of the public service. That is the standard which anybody would advise for the conduct of any private business, and, in so far as is possible, that is the standard which should be adopted by the Government in respect to the expenditures of any particular department. The Postmaster General sought to justify this increase in his expenditure by the reason that he was called upon to engage in extraordinary expenditures in connection with rural mail delivery, in connection with additional railway mail subsdies, and in connection with increased pay to  -
the civil servants of his department According to the figures he gave, this would account for an annual increase of about $1,250,000. But we find that the increased expenditure of 1915 over 1914 was just about $3,000,000; so the $1,250,000 does not account for the full additional expenditure. He says further that he was obliged to make unusually large expenditures because of increased business in places like Montreal, Toronto and Quebec. I do not know what business he referred to as having increased. It was certainly not the business of the Post Office Department, because the revenues did not increase very substantially at any of these places. For instance, the gross revenue at Quebec in 1914 was $184,362, and in 1916,	$213,563; at Montreal, in 1914,
$1,625,000, and in 1915, $1,590,000; at Toronto, in 1915, $2,703,000, and in 1915, $2,905,000. These figures certainly do not indicate any increase worth speaking of at these important points. Surely we can have some slight increases in the revenues of a department without necessitating an increase in the expenditure. The increase in the gross revenue at these three points was very small indeed; so this reason given by the Postmaster General the other night that the increased expenditure was due to increased business at certain points does not hold good. He has signally failed to account for the alarming deficit -in his department. It is all very well to say that expenditures have increased; they are expected to increase in the Post Office Department, I suppose; but let us not forget that the revenues have also increased very substantially. The Postmaster General is looking merely at one side of the account. He would have us believe that the revenue was constant and that he had to meet unexpected and unusual expenditures which was responsible for a deficit of $3,000,000 last year, and probably $5,000,000 this year. My hon. friend from Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) suggests that a gTeat deal of the revenue secured by the Department during the past year, under a strict accounting, should not be credited to the Post Office Department. However, I do not propose to discuss that particular point this afternoon.
I made the statement some time ago that the system of letting our mail contracts by tender had been practically abandoned by this Government. The Postmaster General did not agree with that statement. He said that the department had strictly adhered to tender and contract, and he thought it a

splendid system. I repeat to-day what I said on two occasions in the past, that the system of tender and contract has been practically abandoned by the present Postmaster General, and more particularly by his predecessor, until now nobody in the country has any confidence whatever in the integrity of the system. I know numbers of people who ordinarily would tender for mail contracts, but who absolutely refuse to do so to-day; and I say the practice of the Government justifies the course of such people. I do not know whether I can at once put my hands upon some evidence I had on this point, but I might refeT to a question put to the Government this session by the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll), and answered by Mt. Cas-grain, as follows:
Q. Who has the contract for carrying the mail between the tram car and the post office at Glace Bay?-A. William Grade.
Q. What remuneration does he receive?-A. $345 per annum.
Q. What was the amount of his tender; who were the other tenderers, and the respective amount of their tenders?-A. Tenders were received from Daniel McIntosh at $350, and Joseph Devoe at $400. Mr. Devoe reduced his tender to $345, and the contract was awarded to him. On account of the enlistment of his son, he withdrew his offer, and the contract was given to William Gracie at the same price.
I have in mind four different cases of just that kind this session, the Government giving the information in reply to questions. One was in answer to the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), who cited a similar case the other day, and so did the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) a few days ago; an answer given to a question by the late Mr. Law was of the same nature-all indicating that the department absolutely disregarded the system of tender and contract. I say the Poet-master General- hae no right to award contracts to persons who are not the lowest tenderers. The Postmaster General has no right to allow a man -whose tender is higher than the lowest to put in a second tender which is lower than the lowest previously in. But it has been done in hundreds and hundreds of cases since 1911, when the present Administration came into power. It was done in scores of cases in the calendar year 1915. I -have personal knowledge of a number of such cases.
t	_
Did it ever occur when the late Government was in power?

Never in my experience as a supporter of the late Administration
164J
did I ask that such a thing be done. It may have been done, but if it was, it was just as reprehensible then as it is now. This country has never had a Postmaster General who disregarded the system of ten-% der and contract to the extent the predecessor of the present Postmaster General did; and I suppose the -staff of the department has been so badly trained in recent years that it would be difficult for them now to revert to more correct methods. I do not know how the evil is to be corrected. One method might be for the Postmaster General to resign and let some one else come in, or he might give the matter his serious and earnest consideration, and see that the practice of tender and contract was not departed from hereafter. I was disappointed when the Postmaster General justified, a little while ago, the awarding of a contract to a person whose tender -was not the lowest. That is not what I expected from a good public administrator. Had he not attempted to justify it, I should have thought that he was not responsible for this very improper and reprehensible practice; but it was quite clear that he sought to justify it, and he even looked around for applause, and received some from hon. gentlemen sitting around him. So I must believe that the Postmaster General is a party to this improper practice.

I think the hon.
member said that the tender was $345 per yeaT. Does he know the distance and how many times a day the mail has to be delivered from the tramway?
I do not think that is important.
It is very important.

There are only two
things to do: you must either respect the system of tender or disregard it. If you frequently disregard it, you might as well abandon it altogether.
I wanted to know if the mail contractors are paid a$ much in my county as they are in my hon. friend's county.

I agree with my hon.
friend that there are many instances whete mail contractors do not receive a sufficient amount.
I think so too.

But whom are they to
blame but themselves? What system can you devise for making mail contracts other than the system of tender3 Would you leave the question to patronage or to the department entirely? If so, T venture to say that instead of the Post Office Department costing $15,000,000 or $11,000,000 yearly, it would cost $35,000,000.

Supposing a contractor had given good service and yet the Post Office Department advertised for tenders and the original contractor's tender was, say, $5 higher than the lowest tender. Does my hon. friend think that there might not be cases like that where one would be justified in allowing the original contractor to lower his price by that $5?

I will answer my hon. friend in this way. In the first place, the supposititious case which he has put is not on all fours with the four cases which I had in mind and which are referred to in Hansard of this session, nor is it like the case which I have specifically referred to. In every mail contract there is always a provision enabling the department to renew it. When a mail service has once been put up for tender, there is nothing left for the department to do but submit to the result of the tenders. It might well happen in many cases that, if the retiring contractor's price was but a few dollars above the lowest tender, the department might be justified in awarding the contract to him for some reason such as the unreliability of the lowest tenderer or something like that. The only security, however, that this country has for a proper administration of the Post' Office Department is the system of tender. If you abandon that system, in a few years you will have the Post Office expenditure consuming half the revenues of the country. In that respect, the Post Office Department is entirely different from the other departments.

Would you advise the
Postmaster General to accept the lowest tenders in all cases?

The law practically
compels him to do so.

There is a rural mail
route in my constituency for which there are three tenders, one, $1,197; another, $1,350; and the third, $1,500.

I would not give the contract to any of them.
[Mr. Sehaffner.J
What would you do in a case of that kind?
That is not a very difficult case;

The maximum amount
in Ontario is $30 per mile. These tenders are away too high.

There is not a great
deal of spread between - the highest and lowest tender in that case, and if the lowest tenderer can give the department the security required by the statute, why should he not receive the contract?
But in this case you are going to pay him more than the business is actually worth, because he is a friend of yours.

Do I understand my
hon. friend to say that the lowest tender is too high?
Yes.

In that case I would noi award the contract at all. It frequently happens, and properly so, that the department declines to give a contract to the lowest tenderer on the ground that the amount' of the tender is excessive. There may have been collusion, as there frequently is, and the minister has in his department some officers who are employed in that work practically all the time.
You speak of collusion. There is no collusion. One tenderer is a Conservative and the other two are Liberals, and the two Liberals are the two high tenderers.

I can hardly apprehend the point that my hon. friend is making, and I do not think he apprehends my argument. During the last two sessions we have repeatedly urged upon the Government the necessity of the greatest possible reduction in public expenditures. We have been doing so because of the unusual conditions which surround us and by reason of our financial necessities. We are not satisfied with the response which we have secured from the Government up to date in regard to our many demands in this re- ' spect. We feel that they have not paid the proper heed to our requests for greater economy in public expenditures.

Where do you suggest that the Postmaster General should start in to economize by reducing expenditure? You have given a general statement; it would

be interesting to know what suggestions you would make to economizing.

It is very difficult for me to answer my hon. friend's question directly. It would require a great deal ol time and study, but I want to point this out to him, that the administration of the Post Office Department has apparently been debauched during the last four or five years. I have not the slightest hesitation in making an estimate of the losses of the department on account of the disregard of the system of tender. I venture to say that the department has added to its expenditures by nearly $1,000,000 just by reason of that.

You are absolutely
wrong.
There are many districts in my province in which the Post Office Department can hardly get persons to tender. How can you expect them to tender when tenders are so diregarded?
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that that system prevails throughout the Dominion? '

I know it does in my province. I noticed, in looking over Hansard a few days ago, a case similar to the one I referred to a moment ago, contained in the answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan). I think, therefore, it is a fair assumption that, if you find a department engaging a certain form of administration in one province, it will be indulging in the same practice in other provinces. I have no doubt that the same practice prevails in other provinces.
Does my hon. friend know that throughout the country the general complaint is that tenders for carrying the mails are let at starvation prices?

The hon. gentleman said the same thing a few days ago and he also boasted of our system of calling for tenders for mail contracts. It may be quite true that many mail contractors are performing services at unprofitable figures, but they are responsible for that condition.
Can my hon. friend give any cases in which the tenders that were accepted were too high, the country thereby losing money?
The department is bound to lose money when it disregards the tender system.

Does my hon. friend mean to say that the department would give the contract to the highest tenderer? I may tell him that that has never happened since I have been Postmaster General, and I do not think it happened before, either.

I do not think that I made the statement that the hon. member did give contracts to the highest tenderers. I was answering a question put to me by the hon. member for Haldim-and as to whether the country was losing anything through a contract being awarded not to the lowest tenderer but to one of the higher tenderers. I say that the department would* lose the difference between the amount of the contract and the amount submitted by the lowest tenderer. The statute requires the Post Office Department to solicit tenderers. In that respect there is a statutory obligation on the part of the Postmaster General. That this has not been done is an unfortunate thing for the department and for the country.

So far as my riding is concerned, the system of calling for tenders has been absolutely carried out in every case. In my riding 50 per cent of the mail contractors are Liberals; the other 50 per cent are Conservatives.
M*r. MACLEAN: I am very glad to hear it. No doubt my hon. friend approves of the .conduct of the Post Office Department in respect to mail contracts so far as his own constituency is concerned. That he is quite satisfied indicates that he does not meddle with the affairs of the department. I trust that he will use his good offices with the Postmaster General with a view to seeing that the same policy is established with respect to other constituencies.
That is the policy in every constituency.

The hon. member for Halifax is right in respect of some cases. I plead guilty to asking that the lowest tender be disregarded in one case where the lowest tender was $1,175-the (distance was 24 miles. The contract was let for $575, and the remuneration is considered to be good.. I think the Government was justified in doing that. The hon. member is justified

in stating that expenses have increased very much. In the county of Dufferin the post office expenses have increased by ' over $17,000 by reason of the establishment of rural mail deliveries. I think that if there is any class of people in Canada today who ought to have satisfactory accommodation in this respect it is the farming community. I do not think there is a member on the opposite side who will disagree with that view.

The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has referred to a case which I was not discussing. If the amount of the lowest tender ie excessive, certainly the tender should he disregarded. It was the intention of the Fathers of Confederation in framing the first Post Office Act that the Post Office Department should be administered practically by statute. Its ramifications were so many that it was thought that for the safety of the department and the country, a system of tendering should be imposed upon the department by law. The less interference in connection with mail contracts that there is on the part of members of Parliament, the better, I think, it is for themselves and for the department. If one goes through many fit the files of the Post Office Department relating to mail contracts he will find that members of Parliament interested in intending mail contractors improperly use their influence with results which are not favourable to the department, and which are financially disastrous to the country.

Then why is the hon.
gentleman interfering?
We know that the Post Office Department will not award a contract until they have first consulted either the Conservative member for the county or the defeated candidate in the last election.

Was that done when the
Liberal party was in power?
Speaking for my own constituency, I say no. I was never consulted by the Post Office Department with regard to any tender after it had been submitted to the department.

My purpose in referring to expenditures was two fold: first to point out to the House that there are many instances in which, without injuring the efficiency of public services, very substantial reductions might well be effected. Secondly,

we should not look only to what are usually referred to as the larger and more important expenditures in the matter of effecting reductions. If the minister of the several departments would investigate in detail the many small expenditures that might be reduced or temporarily abandoned they would in the aggregate effect such economies as would reduce very substantially our total expenditures. It is only too true that additional revenues must be secured, (and the only way to secure additional revenue is by imposing fresh taxation on the people. But when we are imposing fresh taxation for war purposes it is our bounden obligation to see that at this critical period, our departmental expenses be reduced to the mimimum amount. It was for the purpose of impressing these facts on the Government that I have ventured to occupy the time of the House at greater length than I had anticipated when I rose this afternoon.

I am sure that my hon.
friend is anxious that the facts should go upsn record. On March 23, page 2181 of Hansard, when the Immigration Estimates were under discussion, the hon. member for St. John made this statement in reference to the Order in Council that we have been speaking about:	"I found the Order in
Council passed in November was published in the newspapers." In several places on the pages of Hansard on this occasion the statement was made that the Order
I do not think that that would apply to the class of officials that I was discussing.

This statement was made in the discussion. It was made by the Minister of the Interior himself, and subsequently by the hon. member for St. John, who said that he had looked it up and found the fact to be as stated. This moment I spoke to the Minister of the Interior on the matter and he said that the Order in Council was passed on the first day of November, just five months ago, and that since that time, in every department of the service, both inside and outside, no double pay has been given by the Government. It would have been only fair if my hon. friend had obtained that information . before he made the statement.	'

Did my hon. friend ask the minister whether or not he had told the House, when discussing the Estimates of the Immigration Department, that one of

the reasons why he had to maintain these figures at such a high point was the fact that money was paid to these officials who were away on active service?

I am making the statement that if my hon. friend was in the House, and if he would look at Hansard, he would see that the minister made the statement that the Order in Council was amended on the 1st of November, 1915, so that no man who enlisted after that date would receive double pay. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) corroborated the statement, saying that he had looked it up and found it to be correct, and had also seen it published in the newspapers.

I thoroughly agree with what has been said by the hon. member for South Bruce (Mr. Truax), that it is high time that the delivery of mails was extended beyond cities and towns to the farmers in the rural districts. I have been able to establish in my constituency only about three rural mail routes in all these years, and the reason I have such difficulty in establishing them is that in every case tenders are called for, and no person can be got to do the work for what the Government is willing to pay. There is the greatest difficulty in getting the mail carried from the trains to the post offices in various towns, because of the small sums which the Government is willing to allow. In my constituency, since this Government came into power, no contracts have been given for carrying the mails between the post offices and stations, or anywhere else, except t* the lowest tenderer.

As a matter ol fact, any one who looks at the record will find-in this I am speaking of my own riding-that the courier service is generally performed by retired farmers or men who have a little money and own horses. They tender at a very low price. No man ever makes a living out of this service, or professed to.
Hear, hear.

At Penetanguishene,
where the post office is fully half a mile from the station, the service, which is four trips a day, is performed for 53 cents a day. Similar cases will be found all through. In the first place, all applicants for these contracts must tender against the hotels in the town, whose bus drivers can throw the mail on the bus and carry it to the post office with really no extra trouble. In Orillia, in my constituency, the courier makes eight
trips a day, and he has to start in about six o'clock and be on duty until well on to midnight, for which he receives $1.66 per day. When my hon. friend from Halifax talks about exorbitant figures 5 p.m. for courier services and men getting contracts without competition, he does not talk within the record.
I was not speaking about exorbitant figures, but simply pleading to have the system of tenders respected.
I know of no case in the last three years in my riding in which the contract has not been 'given to the lowest tenderer, whether he be a Liberal or a Conservative.

I think the most serious part of the charge of the hon. member for Halifax was that when three or four men tendered the contract was not given to the lowest tenderer, but that the highest or some favourite was communicated with and asked to reduce his tender to a little below that of the lowest tenderer, and the contract was then given to him.
Where was that?

That was in the case mentioned at Glace Bay and in other cases. As a matter of fact, I know that this has been done in several cases in my own province, and it has become so common that a great many people think it is of no use to tender, because if they do not stand in well with the Conservative member or the defeated candidate, even if their tender is the lowest, they will not receive the contract.
Can my hon. friend give one instance in his own constituency in which the mail contract is let for a price which is too high?
No, that is not the charge.
Oh yes, it is.
The Postmaster General, just a few moments ago, stated that the mails were carried for a very low price, that in many instances the work was done for prices that were too low.
Then where does the public interest suffer?

Well, the public interest suffers in this, where does the fairness come in when a special man is communicated with and asked to reduce his tender, when he is informed that he must bring it down to a certain figure before he will be

allowed to enter into a contract with the department? The system of tendering is done away with; it is simply a farce.
What proof has the hon. gentleman that the tenderer was communicated with?
He must have been communicated with.
Oh, oh.
The Postmaster General will not deny that.
That is only an allegation made by yourself.

I know it as a matter of fact, and the hon. gentleman knows it, if he is qualified to give an opinion on this subject at all. The Postmaster General knows that it is done. How otherwise would the highest tenderer reduce his offer to a figure a little 'below that of the lowest tenderer unless he was communicated with and given the figures of the lowest man? There is no other way in which it could be done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: ''Might I remind the House that the motion is for the second reading of Bill No. 74, an Act to levy a Tax on Business Profits.

The discussion has drifted off into matters of detail, but it was understood, as the hon. member for Halifax has said, that the general condition of the country might be reviewed at this time on this measure, which, after all, is a measure for raising revenue for the Government. First, let me say that the evidence as to gentlemen who are not members of this House being continually consulted by the Post Office Department as to whether contracts should be awarded to certain persons, is contained in numerous returns which have been brought down to the House by the Postmaster General; and I may say for the information of my hon. friend that I shall be glad to submit to him several returns brought down by the Postmaster General relating to post office matters in my constituency, from which it can be seen that the practice of the department is to [DOT]continually consult some gentlemen in that constituency for advice in regard to that subject. One would think, to hear hon. gentlemen, particularly the hon. memoer for Dufferim (Mr. Best) discussing this question, that because it costs this country $17,000 more to carry the mails in his county

than it used to do, that was a very meritorious thing in this year of grace, 1916.
The Minister of Finance, in his Budget speech of this, year, reiterated the absolute necessity for economy in regard to every phase of public administration in this country, and the necessity of dispensing with all expenditures that might not be deemed absolutely essential. I submit that where you have in one constituency an increase of $17,000 for the carrying of mails, you have a case, not of economy, but of reckless disregard of the principle which the Minister of Finance declares to be absolutely essential.
Was the increase all in one year?
That was the statement given by the hon. member for Dufferin; I am merely quoting what he said.
The increase alluded to was in connection with rural mails.
I know that.
The only way in which it could be reduced would be to withdraw rural mail delivery from the farmers of the country.

My hon. friend need not have any misunderstanding about my position. I db not propose to withdraw rural mail delivery. The Minister of Finance is right when he says that we must economize, and my hon. friend ;(Mir. Bowman) need not make appeals to class, or to the farmers particularly. He need not allege that it is .a great thing to go on being a 'spendthrift in providing rural mail delivery, and that because the Government are spendthrifts in increasing mail routes we should not S'ay anything about it.

I may say that the reason for the increase was created before the war, that is, the rural mail delivery system was introduced before the war. That being so, how could you possibly reduce that expenditure without withdrawing rural mails from the people of the country?

I am not speaking about withdrawing anything that existed before the war. My hon. friend admits that if the increase of rural mails means extravagance, then it is something entirely different from economy. The situation is this: My bon. friend thinks that the Min-

ister of Finance should not economize in regard to rural mails 'but should be a spendthrift.
Certainly not, but 1 think that rural mail should not be withdrawn.

My hon. friend can discuss this when I get through. He asked me a question, and I stated my position. He says that, because rural mails were instituted before the war began, we should not take them away. I do not propose to>
withdraw them, but I say to the Minister of Finance that there is no use in talking about economizing in this or that department, if he is going to permit the Postmaster General and his department, whether in regard to rural mails, or in regard to anything else, to abnormally increase the expenditure. That is not economy. Of what use is it for the Minister of Finance to say:
From this viewpoint it is our true policy to augment our financial strength by multiplying our productive exertions, and by exercising a rigid economy which reduces to the minimum all expenditures upon luxuries and non-essentials.
I care not in what department it may ibe; you can make a specious argument about the desirability of this improvement, or of that, which on account of the war has become a luxury, but when you make that argument you are running counter to the views of the Minister of Finance, who declared that rigid economy is absolutely needed to-day.

Would it be the policy of my hon. friend not to establish any rural mails at all during the wax?
(Mr. MACDONALD: If the financial position of this country is, as I understand it to be, and as the Minister of Finance says it is, then the establishment of new rural mail routes in this country, having become a luxury, should he suspended until this country returns to its normal condition. The Minister of Finance will not take the responsibility of saying that my position in that regard is not correct.
What is the position of my hon. friend in regard to this matter? The Minister of Public Works says, " hear, hear." Probably he would do in regard to those Estimates,-which the Minister of Finance is not going to spend, which have only been put in to bedooked at, or spent only in cases of strictest necessity,-what he did
on a previous occasion where an estimate for a post office was put in before the war and left in the Estimates since the next year, and some one having whispered to the Minister of Public Works that it would be desirable to buy a site as a matter of political importance and necessity, he last year, when this country was struggling with the necessities of war, struggling with the problems which are today looming up more distinctly on the horizon, to please political friends, proceeded to buy the site for a new post office building, so as

Mr, ROGERS: If I remember the case rightly, it was that expropriation proceedings had started before the war in connection with the site, and they were carried out.

people to-day? For the first time, direct taxation has been imposed upon the Canadian people within the last year. For the first time the tax-gatherer has gone round, and business people and others have been asked to contribute immediately and directly from their revenues to the finances of the country. In order to provide for the extravagance, which my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) pointed out, the Postmaster General proceeded to appropriate the proceeds of the sale of war stamps sold through his department. I submit to the Minister of Finance that, in regard to that matter, he should provide that the sale of war stamps be through the Inland Revenue Department. Then we would have an opportunity of ascertaining just how much money was received from that source, and how much taxation the people were paying directly in that way on account of the waT. My hon. friend the Postmaster General takes all the money derived from the sale of these extra stamps, includes it in his general receipts, and nobody can. tell how much has been paid; it is lost track of. If my hon. friend had done as he ought to have done, if he had provided for the sale of these war-tax stamps through the Inland Revenue Department, just as he provided for the sale of those other stamps from which the country gets revenue, for inland revenue and excise purposes, the country would know where the tax was coming from, would be in a position to trace it and would be able to ascertain whether is was being properly applied. Instead of that it is absorbed by the Postmaster General and it is absolutely lost in so far as its original purpose to help the w;ar expenditure is concerned,
This country stands face to face with four great problems. First, there is this tremendous expenditure that is rendered necessary by the war and as to the necessity of which we are all agreed. The Minister of Finance will be bound to agree with my proposition to him, that in regard to the expenditures which are made for the war, the most careful scrutiny should be exercised. We have just finished debating a problem in this House regarding that phase of the subject. What is the use of my hon. friend urging a "rigid economy which reduces to the minimum all expenditures " unless the greatest care is exercised in regard to the. honest expenditure of money for war purposes?
'Then we have a railway problem in this country. As I said a few moments ago, 
we hear rumours in and about the House of Commons of the Government coming to this Parliament before it prorogues and asking us to assist some of the great transcontinental railways. The problem is a very serious one. Already the commitments of Canada in regard to the Canadian Northern railway are of the most onerous character. We have not up to this time seriously considered, as we ought to have done, what these commitments are, how they should be worked out and what has become of the guarantees which the Government has given in connection with that enterprise. There is in addition to that a rumour as to assistance to a railway in Quebec and as to assistance to the Grand Trunk Pacific. If my hon. friend the Minister of Finance proposes in this session to ask this country to make further commitments in regard to these enterprises, when our finances are subject to great stress, is it possible for him to declare that economy in post office expenditure is not essential in the interest of the country? It does seem to me that some hon. gentlemen opposite do not yet realize as they should that the financial position of Canada is of such a character that the words of the Minister of Finance must be respected. But the great trouble with the Minister of Finance in regard to this matter is that he does not convince either the House or the country of his sincerity when he preaches economy. With one hand we provide for a propaganda for economy' that is to be undertaken while he makes the announcement that he allows $20,000,000 to $25,000,000 to remain in the Estimates under these conditions :
Our Estimates contain numerous items hitherto adopted by Parliament, representing works with which it is not our intention to proceed during the period of the war. The policy adopted from its outbreak, which has given such excellents results to date, of proceeding only with works actually under contract, will continue to guide us.
If my hon. friend is sincere in that profession of economy, why does he keep these extravagant and unnecessary items in his Estimates? There is no use of any one starting out to assert the necessity of economy in his household if he has the money in his pocket and shows that he does not intend to economise, and notwithstanding the financial situation in which he may happen to be at this moment or at the outbreak of the war, starts into a line of absolutely reckless expenditure? That is what the Minister of Finance is doing. His

position is that having $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 in my Estimates here, I want the country to understand that although I am talking about economy, I can spend that money if I want to, because I have it in my power to spend it if I chose to do so; there is no restraint on my spending it if I desire to do so, and I ask you to give me the money and make it available for me to spend if 1 see fit-that is what the Minister of Finance says. Yet he asserts that he desires to be economical. When it is said that this $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 should be taken out of the Estimates, some hon. gentlemen say: Oh, well, you cannot tell whether the war will end within a few months. I want to ask the Minister of Finance-and I suppose he will be speaking on this subject before the discussion concludes-to be frank enough to tell us whether, if the war does end, he would venture to undertake the expenditure of any portion of that $20,000,300 or $25,000,000 before the end of this financial year? The Minister of Finance will not venture to take that position. The commitments of this country in regard to the war, and the possible commitments in regard to railways and other conditions in this country, the Finance Minister himself knows will never permit him, within this financial year to 'spend this $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 if he carries out that programme of economy which he lays down for himself and the people of Canada. If that is so, why does he put it there? Why is he not frank with the House and with the people? I am told that the Minister of Finance has announced that he is going to spend a large amount of money upon a newspaper propaganda in regard to economy. He might as well save every cent of that money in regard to this newspaper propaganda if he is going to leave that $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 in the Estimates, while on the one hand preaching economy and on the other having this money spent if political pressure compels him to do it. That is the situation. We have the war and we have the possible railway commitments. We have the financial situation which was exposed to the House by my hon. friend in his Budget, and which we discussed when that Budget was brought down in February. But what have we in addition to that? We have thrown upon the people of Canada at this time, in order that we might he prepared for our future, certain necessary requirements to which we must pay particular regard. We must do something to further our agricultural and mineral developments. In order that the financial equilibrium of
the country may be 'maintained, in order that when the war stress is over, when the world resumes its ordinary avocations and our people once more are engaged in their old employments, we must have lines of policy laid dbwn in reference to agricultural and mineral developments along which we can advance. But, the Minister of Finance comes along and strikes at the mining industry. He says that it is a matter for congratulation that he did not strike at the farmers and he thinks he should be applauded for that. But while he does that with one hand, he strikes at the mining industry with the other. He has introduced a Bill which, if it had passed in the form in which it was presented to the House, would have absolutely prevented, as the minister knows very well, any development of the mining industry in this country. It is true that my hon. friend has so amended the provisions of the Bill that he is going to take into consideration the ore in the mine; and he will, no doubt, congratulate the country upon the fact that 'by reason of these amendments, the mining industry will not be injured at all. That has been his attitude from the day he brought down the Budget; nobody was going to be hurt; only one or two men would he affected to any material degree. But I maintain that these proposals are a menace to every person, not only in this country, but elsewhere, who is interested in the mining industry.
