The Government, instead of frittering away the revenues of this country on the building of a wharf here, anc^ the construction of a 'building there, should, at a time like this, direct its 'expenditures along some definite line of the country's proper development, and in that way bring about results of the greatest possible importance to the country.
I have received a telegram from the Ross-land Board of Trade giving their views on this Bill, and I might take this opportunity of reading it to the House:
Rossland, B.C., March 29, 1916.
E. M. Macdonald, M.P.,
Ottawa.
At a meeting of the Rossland Board of Trade resolution was unanimously passed recommending- that the new war tax Bill he amended by taxing incomes over $2,000, and taxing personal property, and that the machinery of each province be used in the collection, thereby saving immense sums, as it was considered that this method was the most equitable; and failing in this, that the minimum capital affected he reduced to $25,000, and the spread between persons and corporations he changed from 3 to

2 per cent, and that the retroactive features apply only to those supplying war materials.
Jesse Kemp,
Secretary, Board of Trade,
Rossland.
The suggestion which these gentlemen make in regard to the retroactive feature seems to me a most reasonable one. If my bon. friend puts into effect the Budget which he has announced, and pushes it to the limit of the powers which are given to him in the Bill which he has submitted, and to which we are asked to give second reading, he will be doing the greatest possible injury by making these taxes retroactive in every case, whether it is a partnership, a firm, an individual, or a corporation. The Minister of Finance, in making these people contribute a percentage of the profits they have made in previous years, is appropriating money to which, according to all the laws of justice and fair play, he has no right.
The Roseland Board of Trade suggests that if the retroactive feature is to come into force, it should apply only to those supplying war materials. They give my hon. friend a reason why he should act in the one case and not in the other. For the first time in the history of this country we have a Minister of Finance interfering with the mineral possibilities of this country, and imposing a tax on an industry which should not be interfered with, unless every other industry amd individual in the country is to be taxed ailso.
I am not going to point out again the discriminatory nature of my hon. friend's proposals. He is leaving wealth in the hajids of scores of people in this country who have never used it for the development of business by which another man might be able to make a dollar. My hon. friend is discriminating in favour of that class, and against those who have money invested in industry. I cannot believe that he will put this taxation into force in the terms in which the Bill empowers him to do it; and it is probable that in the months to come, when he finds out how unpopular the taxation is, 'he will attempt to deal with it as he did with those items in the Estimates which he told us were put in only for show and were not intended to be expended. For a long time we have been endeavouring to find out which were the items that were not to be expended. Just imagine a Finance Minister putting an item of a quarter of a million dollars in the Estimates to provide for the carrying on of a Geodetic
I Mr. Macdonald.]
Survey to define the boundary between New Brunswick and the United States' Imagine the enormity of it! He is also asking Parliament to vote $1,000,000 for the Yukon, where there are only 8,000 people; that means that the people of Canada will have to pay every one of these 8,000 people, men, women, and children, a bonus of $12C to $125 for the purpose of remaining in the Yukon. Why, it is absolutely farcical. Will my hon. friend say there is any justification for the expenditure of a quarter of a million dollars on t-he Geodetic Survey? What sense or use is there in a proposition of that kind at a time like this? I have given two conspicuous examples that have been disclosed as we have taken up the Estimates, and I could cite other instances along the same line. Items of a similar character were disclosed in the Estimates of the Minister of Mines only a few days ago. It does seem to me that the Minister of Finance paid no attention to the preparation of these Estimates at all, except perhaps to ask each minister to he a little careful, and it depended on the whim and humour of the different ministers whether any care was taken in drawing up the Estimates. The Minister of Finance simply placed his imprimatur on the Estimates proposed, and they were then laid on the Table. Yet all the time the Minister of Finance was going about preaching economy, telling us how necessary it was to be prudent in our public and private expenditures. He expected the people oi this country to take him at his word, while he allowed these anomalous and farcical propositions that I have mentioned, to remain in the Estimates. He expects the people to allow themselves to be taxed undeT this taxation measure without resenting it; tout I venture to say that they are thinking perhaps more deeply in these war times than ever before, and my hon. friend must not assume that, because he sailed along with good luck for two years, he is going to escape that close scrutiny and careful examination of his financial proposals and his expenditures which will certainly be given by the people of this country this year. Every day we are coming nearer to the point when, owing to the enormous expenditures occasioned by the war, it will not be necessary for the Minister of Finance to preach economy, because the people will have to practise it, and when they have to practise it and the stern reality is forced home upon them as to the condition of things, they

will realize how fictitious is the economy which the minister has suggested in his Budget of this year and in the Estimates *which he has presented to the Canadian people.
I mention three lessons which it is important for the people of this country to take into consideration at the present time: the necessities of the war; the railway problem and how it is to toe solved, and the necessity of having close regard to the development of agriculture and of our mineral resources. There is another matter to which I wish to refer. My hon. friend has apparently never paid the slightest attention to how the produce of this country is to be carried to markets across the ocean. The mercantile marine of Canada and of Great Britain has been almost swept off the seas. In Canada the problem of transportation by land, so far as the facilities apart from the financial problems are concerned, has been solved and well solved, so far as our requirements for the next twenty years are concerned, by the construction of three transcontinental lines. But if you scrutinize the Estimates carefully, you will find out that gross extravagance characterizes Civil Government, and characterizes this matter and that matter along lines that do not mean a return to this country of a single advantage; you will find further that this Government has never moved one foot along the line of providing adequate facilities for transportation across the ocean. Of what use are the crops in our western land and our mineral resources, those two essential things out of which Canada must get the money with which to pay her bills when the war is over, if the murmurings which we already hear from our western friends as to the lack of facilities for ocean transportation are found to be based upon stern realities? The day is near when we shall find that we have no ships in which to carry our produce across the ocean. Hon. gentlemen who do not live near the sea-and I say it without any feeling of disparagement to them-do not realize perhaps as keenly as do we who live in the Maritime Provinces how acute the problem is. We realize that the situation is imminent, and is one which any Government ought to be prepared to face with a greater degree of consideration than any other -situation that faces the Canadian people at the present time.
My hon. friends might well revise his Estimates; he might economize in regard to millions of dollars that he has placed in them and proceed with expenditures that will provide for adequate facilities for transportation across the ocean, which will be the great necessity during the next ten years, as any one who thinks must realize. Of what use will our agricultural or our mineral wealth be if, when we have taken it to our ocean front on either side of this country, we are met by the handicap of having no mercantile marine directly or indirectly interested in it which will enable us to provide for the ocean transportation of our products. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has not in his Budget shown an appreciation of the importance of them. In his Estimates he has not shown economy; in his taxation measures he has not provided a scheme by which taxation will be evenly distributed; his taxation measures are discriminatory in their nature between our mineral industries and our ordinary industries, whereas they should be imposed in such a way as to be evenly distributed throughout the country. My hon. friend has fallen short of the duties imposed upon him at this serious juncture in our history in that he has shown himself, in these measures which he has submitted to this House and to the country, incapable of dealing with the problem in an adequate manner.

Just for a few moments I wish to speak upon the reckless extravagance of- the language of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). I have been amazed and disconcerted at his attack upon the Post Office Department in relation to -rural mail delivery. If there is in this country one class of people entitled to consideration and to the development of the means of correspondence and of transacting their business; if there is one class that is entitled to more attention than it has hitherto received in this country, surely it is the farming class,. My hon. friend has been wearing away the weary hours this afternoon by reckless vituperation of a department that is doing everything it possibly can for the transaction of the business of this country. In one moment he has been condemning extravagance and in the next asking for it. Such absurdities should be done away with. It is time for us to speak and. act like men. There is a very great difference between the speech of the hon. member for Pictou and that of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) who spoke this afternoon with deliberation, and in a commonsense way ap-

pealed to the people to give careful consideration to the questions at issue, instead of devising, as the hon. member for Pictou did, a wild, whirlwind of talk that had no bearing upon any subject on earth, except, perhaps, to disconcert the Postmaster General in the arduous duties which he is called upon to perform. As a farmer and as a representative of the farmers, knowing whereof I speak, I desire to say that I hope there will 'be no further economies which would restrict the distribution oi rural mail. Our farmers are entitled to better and more generous treatment than they are receiving at the present time, and 1 hope there will be no successful attempt to scare the Postmaster General into that absurd thing called economy in connection with such a public service as this which affords absolutely necessary facilities to the farmers of Canada to transact their business.
They will not scare me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Pictou and the hon. member for Halifax have referred to the expenditures, actual and proposed, of the Government. As I stated in my Budget speech, this is essentially a time for economy, but I submit that from the outbreak of the war the Government has exercised that economy, and I think I can prove it to the satisfaction of the House and of the country.
At the outbreak of the war in August, 1914 the policy of the Government as enunciated in the Budget speech was that works under contract should be carried on. The industry of the country had been somewhat dislocated by the war; there was considerable unemployment, and we regarded it in the public intered that those works which were under contract should be continued. That policy was continued during 191a and is in effect to-day. Apart from the war, in connection with which our expenditures will be increasingly heavy, it has been the settled policy of the Government to proceed only with works under contract and with such other works as are indispensably necessary in the public interest, and with no others. Let us see what has been accomplished under that policy. For the fiscal year which ended on the 31st day of March, 1914, a few months before the outbreak of the war, the total expenditures of the Dominion were over $180,000,000. For the fiscal year which ended on the 31st day of March, 1916, our 
expenditures, including a very large amount of interest which we were obliged to pay upon our war expenditure, amounted to $165,000,000. The estimate of our expenditure for the fiscal year 1916-17 apart from the war 'is $160,000,000. Let me point out to the House the significance of these figures. Included in the $160,000,000 which is the estimated expenditure for the fiscal year 1916-17 is $37,000,000 of charges upon the public debt. In 1912 the charges in connection with the public deibt were only about $13,000,000; in 1914, before the outbreak of the war, they were only about $14,000,000. By reason of our expenditure upon the war, we shall have to face for the coming year interest on public debt to an amount oi $37,000,000. Taking the $160,000,000 estimated expenditure for the fiscal year 1916-17 in the light of that statement, we find that if wA subtract the increased charges on public debt due to the outbreak of the war we get an expenditure (other than for war) in the neighbourhood of $135,000,000 for the coming fiscal year. What was the position when this Government assumed power in 1911? The Estimates of the fiscal year 191MB were the Estimates of the late Liberal Administration. I desire to call ithe attention of the House to the fact that the Estimates presented by the late Administration on December 2, 1910, and on May 9 and 'May 17, 1911, amounted to about $157,000,000. Yet, Mr. Speaker, out estimated expenditure for the coming fiscal year, embracing as it does an item ot $37,000,000 fOT interest and charges upon our public debt, an increase of some $23,000,000 over the interest and charges upon the public d'ebt for the fiscal year preceding the outbreak of war, and of some $25,000,000 over the interest and charges upon the public debt for the year 1911-12, our estimated expenditure for the coming year is only $3,000,000 in excess of the Estimates of the late Liberal Administration in 1911-12.

My hon. friend will admit, I suppose, that there is a difference between a time when a war is on and a time when no war is on. Nearly all arguments have been in favour of strict economy because there is war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend mean to say that there was riotous extravagance when the late Government was in power-that there was no economy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The figures which I gave before six o'clock referred to our expenditures for purposes other than the war. I pointed out that the Government had endeavoured to effect all possible economy. For the fiscal year ending March 31, 1915, our total expenditure upon ordinary capital account was $187,000,000. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1916, that expenditure had dropped to $165,000,000. The Estimate for the coming year, that is the fiscal year which began on April 1, 1916, and will terminate on March 31, 1917, is $160,000,000. I pointed out also that in that Estimate was embraced as large an amount as $25,000,000 for interest and charges upon public debt, due to our heavy war borrowings. I also point out that, included in the Estimates for the coming year, are some $3,000,000 for pensions. So I think that, apart from our expenditures upon the war, the figures indicate that the Government has put forth a strong effort to reduce it's ordinary capital expenditures. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) referred to the figures of 1911-12. If I refer to them it is not with the object of instituting any comparison between the record of the present Government and that of the late Government. It does not appear to me that this is a proper occasion upon which to do that, and for the most part such comparisons serve no very useful purpose; at least that is my view. But in connection with the matter of expenditures in ordinary times, it is to be pointed out that in any country, in a period of great material development such as Canada was going through for many years previous to the outbreak of the war, increases in expenditure in all departments of Government are to be expected. In that connection I may be permitted to quote the view of my predecessor, the hon. Mr. Fielding, expressed in his Budget speech of 1904: He said:
X have on several occasions, in referring to decrease which we have been able to show, pointed out that no Finance Minister in a country like Canada need be ashamed if he has to come before Parliament and acknowledge

that he is increasing the public debt. That ought to be the normal condition in a young country like ours, with vast resources to develop, with improvements all around us waiting to be done, and with courageous men ready to do them.
Our expenditure for the year 1911-12, upon the Estimates of the late Government, was about $135,000,000, the Estimates being about $158,000,000. There was a large programme of public works under way, and many large undertakings of national magnitude; and from 1911 until the outbreak of the war, there was undoubtedly a steady increase in the expenditure of the Dominion Government upon ordinary capital account. We had such undertakings on capital account as the National Transcontinental railway, the Quebec bridge, the St. Lawrence ship channel, afterwards the Halifax terminal, the Hudson Bay railway and later the Welland canal. So that, as I have stated, we had a large capital programme under way at the time of the outbreak of war. Our ordinary expenditures had also increased with the development of the country, and in this connection, as showing that a comparison between our expenditures before the outbreak of the war and the expenditures of 1911-12 could hardly be regarded as fair, I desire to point out that the total trade of Canada in 1911 was seven hundred and fifty million dollars. That total had increased to over one thousand million dollars in 1914. There was a slight reduction owing to the war in 1915, but for the fiscal year which has just terminated the total trade will undoubtedly aggregate over twelve hundred million dollars, so that the trade of Canada, the imports and exports of the Dominion, have almost doubled in the five years since 1911 to 1916. Some attention has been .paid to the matter of expenditures in the Immigration Department. I think it is only fair to the department to point out that there was a steady increase in immigration up until the year of the outbreak of the war. In 1910 the immigrant arrivals were 208,000; in 1911 they were 311,000; in 1912 they were 354,000; in 1913 they were 402,000; in 1914 they were 384,000; and in 1915 they were 144,000, whereas for the first 11 months of the fiscal year 1916, the immigration had dropped off, owing to the war, to 42,000. In addition to the expenditures upon various services of the Government, we had a fairly large programme of harbour and port development work that necessarily followed upon the railroad policy which had been adopted by the previous Government. We had one trans-
continental line completed, but with many extensions being built, and two further transcontinental lines in process of completion. It was absolutely necessary, if these three transcontinental lines were to operate successfully, that there should go hand in hand with their completion a development in the	ports of Canada.
Consequently, we had large expenditures to face at Halifax, St. John, Quebec, Montreal, Vancouver and Victoria. As the result of the responsibilities which devolved upon us to meet the public need, our expenditures grew from $135,000,000 in 1911-12 to $187,000,000 for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1915. I am excluding war expenditure, I am dealing only with ordinary and capital expenditure.
The question of the public debt has been touched upon, and may be touched upon later in the course of this debate. Without attempting to draw any comparison between the records o.f the two parties in that regard, because I do not believe that sound conclusions can be drawn from the mere fact of an increase or decrease in the public debt-the question is, for what purpose public debt has been increased rather than whether or not it has been increased as a matter of fact I find that the public debt in 1908 stood at $277,000,000, in 1909 at $323,000,000, in 1910 at $336,000,000, in 1911, at $340,000,000. It dropped in 1912 to $339,000,000, in 1913 to 314,000,000, and in 1914 to $335,000,000. I desire to point out that on 31st of March, 1914, that is at the end of fiscal year preceding the outbreak of war, the national debt of Canada was less than it had been in 1911.
I come now to the year of the war, 1914-15. By reason of the reduction in our revenues, principally after the outbreak of the war, and of our war expenditures which amounted to about $60,000,000 for the year in question, there was an increase in the national debt of $113,000,000. Since the outbreak of war, the responsibility of the Government has, of course, greatly increased. When the war broke out, there were various opinions as to its probable duration. Some thought that it would not last more than six months; others mentioned a year; others again thought that two or three years might elapse before it could be concluded. We determined to do our full duty by Canada and the Empire by putting forth our maximum effort. But at the time, not knowing what the future held, we aimed, in the first instance, at a force of 25,000 men. Some 33,000 men assembled at Valcartier

and were sent overseas. The appropriation in the August session of 1915 for war purposes was $50,000,000. That indicated our view of the effort which we should immediately put forth.
The 50,000 men grew to 100,000, and in 1915 the War Appropriation Bill was for $100,000,000. The 100,000 men grew to 200,000, and then to 250,000, and to-day there have been recruited, and are overseas, or under arms in Canada, no less than 300,000 men. The Appropriation Bill of this year will provide for $250,000,000 of the expenditure, and, as stated in my Budget speech, we shall he faced, during the coming year, with the task of raising in the neighbourhood of $225,000,000 'by borrowing.
In my Budget speech I did not attempt to minimize the seriousness of. the financial situation:	At the same time, I believed
then, and I believe now, that, with the resolution which her people are displaying, Canada can meet, and readily meet, the increased expenditure which will 'be required to equip, send forward and maintain our. army of 300,000, or 350,000, or whatever number we may succeed in enlisting. I have no doubt whatever [DOT] as to that, but, while that is so, the expenditure is, of course, very heavy. It is heavy in comparison with expenditures of the past; it will be heavier six months from now than it is to-day, and, if the war lasts, it will be heavier next year than this. But we are all prepared for that, and the people are willing and even eager to make whatever sacrifice may be necessary in order that Canada, in this crisis in the affairs of the Empire, may do her full duty. I think that is common ground.
The general financial policy which, as Minister of Finance, I have tried to work out is this: I have thought it well that the Dominion should finance well in advance. No one can tell from day to day, and from week to week, what will happen. The financial situation may change overnight, and, therefore, if is a sound policy, even at the risk of losing some interest upon your bor rowing, to borrow well in advance, two or three, or four, months in advance, because, it might chance that, if you pursued a different policy, and borrowed, so to speak, as you immediately required, market conditions might develop in which you might not be able to borrow, and the consequence might be serious. Therefore, I think it is sound financial policy to borrow well in advance of your requirements in war time, and to take advantage of
favourable market conditions as they arise. As the result of that policy we have been successful in financing up to date, and, at the present time, we are financed for many months ahead, so that, while the financial responsibility which we are assuming is seriousi, I believe the country is well able to sustain it.
The second principle which I have adopted is this: that short date loans * should be avoided as much as possible. At the outbreak of the war it was not possible to avoid short date loans, but securities should be issued for reasonably long dates, I would say for as long dates as possible, because it is not desirable during the progress of a war that maturities should have to be met, possibly at a time when fresh borrowing is required for the purposes of the war. Nor is it desirable that after the war, when we are in a period.of dislocation and more or less of reconstruction, heavy liabilities should be falling due. That is the time when I think the Dominion should have the full value of such credit as she possesses to take whatever steps may be rendered necessary by the existing situation.
The third principle is that we should keep expenditures for purposes other than war within as reasonable bounds as possible, and that we have endeavoured to do. When the war broke out, As I stated in the early part of my remarks, there was a serious derangement of business and much unemployment, and I think it was of great advantage to Canada at that time that the Dominion Government had under way a large programme of public works. That fact greatly minimized the unemployment situation.
Reference has been made to the Estimates, not only upon this debate but upon other occasions when the subject was under consideration by the House. When I made my Budget speech I spoke as follows:
As regards our ordinary and capital expenditure, we shall endeavour to continue to effect all possible reductions. Our Estimates contain numerous items hitherto adopted by Parlia-. ment, representing works with which it is not our intention to proceed during the period of the war. The policy adopted from its outbreak, which has given such excellent results to date, of proceeding only with works actually under contract, will continue to guide us. Further, should financial exigency so require, we shall not hesitate to terminate contracts and leave works in an unfinished condition, notwithstanding the immediate and prospective loss and damages involved. I do not, however, think that such a course will be necessary.
That represented the views and intentions of the Government. Should the exigency

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On acount of
war conditions. The war has imposed additional duties and responsibilities upon all the members of the Government, and upon nearly all departments of the Government. In my own department the work devolving upon me as minister has been multiplied many fold. The Department of Finance since the outbreak of the war has had exceedingly heavy responsibilities, and we have had to add to our staff in order to take care of the great commercial loan and other work devolving upon us by reason of the war. I have been in business for some years, and I may say that if as great 'an increase had taken place in the business of any private concerns throughout the country, there would have been a much greater increase of the staff than has been the case . in my department. In many cases the men in my department have frequently worked day and night since the war broke out, in connection with the handling of the gold for the Bank of England, in connection with the financing of the Dominion, and in connection with our loan. There is not a doubt about it that much heavier responsibilities are devolving upon, I believe, most departments of the Government, if not all, than before the war; and simply by reason of the war. I believe the Post Office Department has heavier duties and responsibilities than before the iwar. The work of the Customs Department, too, by reason of the tariff of 1915 and the embargo upon goods of various kinds going out of Canada, and in scores of other ways, is much greater than before t,he war. I am satisfied that the duties of the Trade and Commerce Department have also been largely increased by reason of the war. One might think that the war had imposed no extra work upon the Inland Revenue Department, but as a matter of fact the duties devolving upon

that department have greatly increased since the outbreak of the war-duties devolving upon it by reason of the Budgets of August, 1914, and of February, 1915. It may be that in some departments there is not the same amount of work to be done as before the war, but, generally speaking, I believe it is true that heavier duties and greater responsibilities have devolved upon the departments of the Government than existed before the outbreak of the war.
The Immigration Department has been referred to. As I have already pointed out, there had been a steady increase in immigration to this country up to 1914, but it began to drop off in 1915, and the figures are of small dimensions since the war broke out. But the Immigration Department has had a great deal to do in the Northwest since August, 1914; heavy duties have devolved upon that department in connection with the seed grain distribution, involving something like $13,000,000 or $15,000,000-1 have forgotten the exact amount. There is this further to be borne in mind. When the^ war broke out some were of the opinion' that it would last only a short time. Now, my view would be that, even at the risk of having an overmanned department for a short time, it would be a mistake to disband such an important staff as that of the Immigration Department. Unless it was believed that they would not be required for a considerable time to come, I do not think it would be good policy to disband the staff of any important department. I do not mean to say that economies cannot be effected; I believe they have been effected, and will be effected. But I think it would be a mistake to adopt such a drastic course as dismissing the staff of an important department, when it might be required again within a few months or a year.
These, of course, are general observations with regard to the several departments of the Government. I do not purpose to go into the details of criticisms which have been offered here, except to say that in my judgment the most important question in this country for many years to come will be the question of immigration, the settlement of the land, and increased agricultural production. If you get immigration, you get the land settled; and if you get the land settled, you get increased agricultural production; and increased agricultural production will solve all the other questions which we have been discussing. Increased agricultural production is the key to the future economic situation 
in this country; It is basic, and fundamental. Increase your agricultural production, and increase in all other business will follow. Increased agriculture production, brought about by the energies of our present farming community, by immigration, and by land settlement, will solve the railway situation, ultimately, in Canada.
I do not believe that it would be wise, in order to effect minor economies, to disband the Immigration' staff at this time. I am only expressing my own view upon that point, as the matter has been raised, and the Minister of the Interior is not here.

What are the present
staff doing to help out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are devoting their energies to immigration. There is a great deal of work to be done now. I repeat that I do not think it would be in the national interest to break up the staff of the Immigration Department, because the question of immigration is one of the most important that we have to deal with, and after the war is over all the energies of the Government should be directed to increasing our immigration, and getting the land settled in order to increase production.
With regard to measures of taxation _ which have been introduced, I desire to make this general observation,^ which I do not think can be successfully <k>nitroverted: There are many nations at war, but I believe that this Government has so administered the affairs of the country since the war has broken out that Canada is taxed less heavily than any other of the Dominions, much less heavily than the United Kimgdpm, and less heavily than any country that is engaged in the war. Let us see with what measures we undertook to meet the heavy responsibility with which we were confronted at the outbreak of the war. In August, 1914, it was not desirable, by reason of the dislocation and disarrangement of business, that any comprehensive measure of taxation should be entered upon. What did we do? We had resort to the duties of customs and of excise upon luxuries, upon sugar, upon 'beer, and upon spirits. That taxation measure was a light one. In order that we might meet the situation without resorting to heavy taxation, we took the opportunity of issuing $15,000,000 of an additional Dominion note circulation. We were able to do that because the financial situation was. so strong, and because we had such heavy reserves of gold. There was no injury done to the

financial situation; in fact, it was benefited by the action we took.
By the following February it was pop sible to adopt a comprehensive scheme of taxation, and we did so. We brought in a scheme of special taxation and a scheme of general taxation. Under the special taxation plan the banks, the trust companies, the loan companies were required to pay special taxation into the Dominion treasury. The tax upon the banks alone amounted to about $1,000,000 a year. Taxes were imposed upon cheques, telegrams, and money orders. Taxation was imposed upon those who could bear it. Then we increased the tariff by 5 per cent British preferential and by 7j per cent general. I was surprised to hear my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean), because he is usually pretty, fair, state that the result of our tariff increase had not been to increase the revenue except, I	think	he said, in so	far asit	was	upon free goods. I dissent entirely from his conclusions.
The Budget of 1915 aimed at a revenue of $150,000,000, and up to March 31, 1916, which was the end of the fiscal year, the revenue of the Dominion under the Budget of 1915 aggregated over $171,000,000, or $21,000,000 or more over the estimate. It cannot, therefore, be said that the Budget of 1915 did not realize the intention and the object which it bad in view.
How much came from the importations under the general tariff? That was the point I was making.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not the figures here; but if my hon. friend will look them up, he will find that the greater portion by far, of the difference between the estimated revenue which we should have had under the old tariff and the revenue which we actually derived was from the increase in the tariff.

The application of the 7J per cent tax on free goode brought in $18,000,000 or $19,000,000 of revenue. I admit that. I was questioning the value of the imposition of the 7J per cent on the general tariff 'as a revenue measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not the figures here nor do I think that my hon. friend has the figures. But there is no question about it, that as there was an additional tax of 7J per cerit upon all imports that came in, with the exceptions set out in the Budget, there must be an increase
by reason of that 7J per cent tax. My hon. friend might argue that more would have come in if the duty had not been imposed; but, as the duty was imposed and collected upon such imports as came in, it does not appear to me that he can demonstrate that no results followed from the imposition of the 7j per cent upon the general tariff. If a return were brought down from the Customs Department showing the amount of revenue derived from the 7J per cent duty and the 5 per cent duty, I think my hon. friend would find that it accounted for by far the major portion of the entire amount of the additional revenue, some forty or fifty million dollars, which was raised under the Budget of last year. That Budget in my opinion was eminently successful. I did not expect that I would realize $171,000,000 from it; I thought if I realized $150,000,000, I would do well, but the results have been beyond our expectations.
Coming to the Budget of this year, and especially to the measure which is now under consideration, the same principle has been carried out. The taxation is upon those who, we think, can well afford to bear it. The hon. member for Halifax has intimated that in his opinion it would have been preferable if it had been upon those individuals, firms and companies engaged in supplying war material and munitions. -
I suggested that the tax upon such as these might be larger than upon others.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me ask my hon. friend whether or not that would be quite, fair. I considered that point, because it would naturally occur to one in drafting a taxation measure in war time. But has my hon. friend thought of this aspect of it? What about those who supplied raw material and semi-manufactured products to those who worked them up into material and supplies which they sold to this or any other Government?
You would get at them under the other provisions of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A steel manufacturer may not be making shells, but he may be making huge profits upon steel sold to those who manufacture the shells. If he made as much money as they did, upon what principle could you say: in the one case we will impose a heavy tax, and in the other case a lighter tax? Take those, for example, who have made large profits on the appreciation in the price of com mo-

dities of various kinds due to the outbreak of the war, and to the demand which sprang up after the outbreak of the war for such goods and commodities. It does not seem to me that discrimination can fairly be made. There are many businesses which have made large profits directly owing to the	war,	and others which have
made large profits indirectly owing to the war, and it is difficult to discriminate as amongst them. A taxation measure should be uniform. This taxation measure, as I have said, should not bear heavily upon the business community. In the first place it exempts all businesses with a capital of less than $50,000.
As to those having a capital of ever $50,000 we say: up to 7 per cent in the case of incorporated companies and up to 10 per cent in the ease of individuals and partnerships, you are exempt from taxation; as to the profits which you make in excess of 7 per cent upon capital in one case and in excess of 10 per cent upon capital in the other, we take one-fourth and leave you three-fourths. I do not believe that any exception can be taken in war time to a measure of that kiqd. It is a much milder measure than the measure adopted by the Imperial Government. I observe from the cabled report of the speech of the Chancellor of the Exchequer that by the Budget which he has just brought down he has increased the excess profits tax in Great Britain. I do not see, therefore, how exception can well be taken to this taxation, which is limited in its duration to December 31, 1917, no more than three payments to be made, one in each year.
It has been pointed out by the hon. member for Pictou that the agricultural interests were excepted,by the Budget and that the statement was made that resort would not be had to taxation upon the property or effects or income of farmers. He indicated that in his view that was a class discrimination. I believe that the course taken in that regard embodies a sound principle. Agriculture is the basic industry of this country. [DOT] Any advantage possessed by agriculture inures to the advantage of the entire community, because all other parts of the community depend upon the agriculturist, whose work is fundamental. As our part in this war is being carried out not only by men afid munitions but also by the resources of the nation, the burden of taxation should be made as light as possible upon the farmer, because upon his efforts no less than upon the efforts of the
fSir Thomas White.]
men in the field and in the munition factories will depend in large measure our success in this war. We asked the farmers to increase production and they responded nobly last year with the greatest crop in the history of Canada. We have asked them since to put forth every effort to increase production, to sow, to plant, to raise everything thejr can in order to enable Canada to sustain the burden of the war and continue to do her duty by herself and by the Empire. We are making that appeal to-day and asking the farmers to increase their production, and it does seem to me that it is proper for us to lay down the principle that we should not impose special war taxation on the farming community.
It has been pointed out that many with large incomes will escape taxation. That is true, but this is not an income tax measure. No doubt a good deal could be said for an income tax measure, but we traversed that ground in the discussion in committee upon these resolutions and I do not purpose going into the matter further, except to say this:	It
must be borne in mind that income taxation is being levied by some municipalities and provinces throughout Canada. It may be that the provinces and municipalities will have to resort in greater measure to income taxation. If it were clearly in the national interest, having regard to our needs, to impose income taxation, I should not hesitate to do it, but I have pointed out that until it is clear that it is in the national interest, having regard to our needs, to impose that taxation the policy should be to trench as little as possible upon the field to which the 9 p.m. provinces alone can resort.
Basing a conclusion upon the returns from the income taxation in the United States, an income tax in Canada would return but a fraction of what we hope to get by this measure. I do not believe that an income tax upon individuals in Canada would produce more than $3,000,000. In the United States, which is a very much more populous and a very much wealthier country, I think the return from the income tax on individuals is between $30,000,000 and $40,000,000-I have forgotten the precise figures. I believe that in Canada we could not hope to get more than one-tenth of that amount, and from that would have to be deducted the whole cost of administration of the measure. As I have stated to the House, the

imposing of an income tax would mean that this Government would havie to organize at this time almost a second Civil Service for the purpose of covering the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific to make an income assessment. As our country is of very large geographical area and of scattered population, the cost of making an assessment would be very great. It has been stated that we might avail ourselves of t'he provincial machinery, but I do not think that that would be feasible or practicable. In the first place, some of the provinces have no machinery for that purpose; in the second place, the municipalities are under the jurisdiction not of the Dominion, but of the Provincial Government, and any system of Dominion taxation would have to be carried out by Dominion and not by provincial or municipal officials. I think, therefore, that the income tax proposal, at all events at the present time, is impracticable.
The hon. member for Halifax and the hon. member for Pictou referred to the mining industry and the effect upon it of this taxation. I think that at the outset the taxation measure was somewhat mis-understod by a portion of the mining community. I am quite satisfied, however, that they now understand the measure; they know that it is and was the intention that an allowance should be made for exhaustion of capital. So far as I can learn-and I am fairly in touch with the mining community-this has been accepted as a fair measure in war time. I do not see on what principle I could exempt mines that are paying huge dividends to shareholders and assess all other businesses in the community. This war is being carried on by us for Canada and for every part of Canada. It is being carried on for the mining industry as well as for the manufacturing industry and for the general business, agricultural and other interests of Canada. I know that the mining community, speaking generally, are desirous of paying a portion of this taxation. I think that a number of prominent mining men would feel disappointed if the mining industry was passed over. Many of them desire to pay a share of the taxation which is rendered' necessary by this war, and that is precisely the position which I would expect them to take. As a matter of fact, comparatively few mines in Canada will have to pay at alii because after allowance is made for exhaustion of capital, after capital and reserves are taken into consideration, and
after the 7 per cent allowance is m'ade, the one-fourth of the balance of net earnings will certainly be no very serious matter for the mining companies of Canada which will come within the provisions of the Act.
My remarks have been somewhat desultory, but I have touched only upon the points raised by the hon. members opposite. I certainly have no exception to take to the spirit or tone of the discussion upon the measure now under consideration; it has been exceptionally fair throughout.
I have derived many useful suggestions from the discussion that has taken place since the Budget was introduced. A measure of this kind has to be brought in more or less rough hewn, because full information is not available on which to perfect it or put it into practical shape. However, since the Budget has been brought down, the resolutions have been improved in many material respects, and I believe that we have now a measure which can be worked out without material injustice to any, el^ss of the community, at comparatively small expense, and I feel that its results will equal all the expectations we have formed of it.

Mr. Speaker, I agree very largely with what the minister has said, but there are some things on which I do not agree with him. Personally I would not expect the Government to cease work on large public undertakings necessary for the well-being of the country unless it was imperatively necessary to do so. I do not think that any member on this side of the House has complained about that sort of public expenditure. What we have complained of is unnecessary public expenditure and the fact that the minister has permitted other ministers to put in the Estimates expenditures which they had no intention of carrying out. The minister has stated that it would be difficult or impossible for the different ministers to keep their Estimates down to what they expected to expend. But there are many items that we have passed during the time we have been in Supply that certainly could have been done without. Take, for instance, the Geodetic 'Survey, mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). That could have been done without in a year of stress such as this, without doing harm to anybody. The expenditure was excused by the Minister of the Interior on the ground that he did not desire

to break. up his staff. But I understand that many additional men have been employed in different departments that are not very busy, and I can see no reason why these men should not have (been transferred to the departments that have had additional work thrust upon them, just as a man conducting a private (business would adjust his staff to suit special conditions. I quite appreciate that the Departments of Finance, Customs and Militia would 'be exceptionally busy, but I do not see why the Post Office Department should require the large increases that have been made in the staffs in cities like Montreal, Toronto, and Quebec, especially as there has been a very slight increase in the post office revenue^ Nor can I see why much of the additional work should not be taken care of by calling upon the existing departmental staffs to work a little harder. Their hours are not-long. If business men required their staffs to work only for the same hours that prevail in the departments here, the increase in the cost of the ordinary .business would eat up all the profits. It is of these increases in the number of civil servants in such times as these that people complain. The minister says that when he suggested economy he really meant economy in all departments. The whole people of the country were prepared, as he said, to .pay tlheir share of the cost of the war, perfectly and absolutely willing to do so. But when they see the departments increasing their staffs, and the civil servants getting to work at 10 o'clock and quitting at 4 or 5 o'clock in the afternoon, the ordinary workingman, who. works from 7 o'clock in the morning until 6 o'clock at night, and the ordinary farmer, who works from 4 o'clock or half past four in the morning until 8 o'clock or 9 o'clock* at night, cannot appreciate the statement that the Government are economizing very much. That is the feeling to-day throughout the country. The feeling is that the Government -should set an example in economy. It is not for us to point out to them how they can do so. Each minister should go over his department and see where he can economize. If something of this kind is not done there will be dissatisfaction throughout the length and breadth of the land among people who work hard for tlheir livings, and in many cases get a poor living at that. That is what we mean toy economizing. It is folly to put in such Estimates as we passed the 
other night for this -museum. We are now occupying the museum and are likely to do so for some time. What is the use of putting in Estimates to buy trash for the museum during the next year? That surely is not an example of economy. The ordinary farmer, for instance, in my. section of the country, is perfectly willing to pay his share of the cost of the war; but if I were to take those Estimates home and; show that we 'had voted $300,000 or $400,000 for a geodetic survey in various parts of the country, that could easily be left over for 5 or 10 years, and for a lot of trash for the museum, such as wooden elephants and whales, or those big wooden things we see in the entrance to this building-and if they cost anything the man who bought them ought to be sent to jail-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Totem poles.
Family trees.

The farmers I represent are not prejudiced or stingy, but if they realized these things they would- want to turn us all out for voting for such expenditures, and to put in somebody else who would not vote for them. As to immigration, I absolutely agree with the minister that now is the time to work out a proper scheme for the reception of immigrants into this, country and for placing them on the land. The -pres'ent immigration staff have done nothing to place immigrants upon the land so 1 far as I can judge. For years and years these immigrants have been brought to this country and dumped in the large cities, and that is the end of the matter, so far as the Dominion Government is concerned. They do not see to it that they are placed on the land. It would be better to have only one hundred immigrants in a year, place them on the land, and give them a good start as citizens, than have 10,000 who would flock to the cities and towns and do no particular good to the country. They are not required in the cities and towns. Our mechanics resent them being there. They only reduce the wages of our mechanics, and they live in a way to which our mechanics are not accustomed. If the hon. minister would see to it that the money expended by the Immigration Department was expended in a common-sense way, in conjunction with the provinces, so that the immigrants could be placed on the land and taught something about farming, which would make them take an interest in the farm, he would take a great step in advance towards the solution of the immi-

gration problem in this country. It would pay us more than we can possibly estimate. But we are not doing that.
If immigration declined to 42,000 last year as against 400,000 in 1914, surely the officers of the department might have been employed in some other department. I would not like to say that these men should be sacked, but I do not agree with the minister when he says that if they were discharged it would be difficult to get them when they might be needed again. We all know that if there is one position open in any department, there are from 10 to 100 applicants for it. There is no trouble in getting men, not a particle.
There are lots of applicants even when the positions are not open.

# Yes, but when they are open Heaven knows there are enough applications. I am not one of those who believe in discharging men because there happens to be a dull time, unless it is absolutely necessary for the safety of the business. At the same time, these men could be. used as every large manufacturer uses his men: when there is slackness in one department, he uses them in another.
J ust a word about the tariff. My hon. friend the minister must bear in mind that a great deal of the increased revenue came from the 71 per cent duty on goods that were formerly free. I also know that there has been an increase Horn the machinery and raw material that had to be imported for the manufacture of war supplies since the war started. It would be almost impossible to calculate the amount of the increase from machinery and ihaterial imported from the United States since the war started for the manufacture of war material. I think it is from that source and from the duty on goods that were formerly free that the minister has got the bulk of his increased revenue, because until last fall ordinary business in the country had not very materially increased. In fact, all last summer there was a great dullness, and in ' the case of some businesses it exists at the present time, but last fall the general run of business improved, and there is no doubt that there has been a considerable increase in the importation of raw materials both from Great Britain and from the United States. Still, if I had the time, I could point to many businesses that have not returned to the normal condition by any manner of means.
. With reference to the present Bill, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance saidand he said it very emphatically- that he believes in uniform taxation. I absolutely agree with him, but is this uniform taxation? That is where I disagree with him. It is not uniform taxation. It is all very well to say that Great Britain is taxing war profits, but, so far as I have read the British Bill, and so far as I understand it, it proceeds on a very different principle from the minister's Bill. They take a period of two or three years previous to the war, ascertain the normal profits of the business during that period, and then take one-half of the increase in the profits during the war period. That is a fair method of taxation in comparison with ours.

Does the hon. member
think that it would help the manufacturers if we took the profits of two years previous to the war as a basis? Those years were probably dull years. Does he think it would be fair to the manufacturers to make the profits of those two or three years the basis, and then take one half of the profits they have made since the war started?

If you took the three
years previous to the war I think it would be fair.
I doubt it.

I am not trying to help the manufacturers. I think the manufacturers who are hit by this tariff are perfectly willing. to pay, but they object to their neighbours not paying. The British system would hit the neighbour who does not pay; that is what I mean.

Who are the neighbours
to whom my hon. friend refers; what class of people are they?

They are the people whose businesses are abnormally capitalized, and the class of people whose capitalization falls below the $50,000 mark. The method suggested would take them both in. I would exempt nobody, and I do not think that anybody asks to be exempted. I believe, as I said at the beginning, that everybody in this country is prepared to pay additional taxation for the purpose of carrying this war to a successful issue. Something has been said about the farmers. I believe that the farmers are just as willing to pay as the manufacturers or the merchants. So far as my experience goes, no class has contributed more largely to the patriotic funds than the farmers. They have taxed themselves. I know that, in Ontario, county

councils and township councils throughout the length of the province have taxed themselves for the benefit of the Patriotic, Red Cross and other war funds, and taxed themselves willingly. I believe that that is their feeling to-day.	.
Coming back to the British tax, I believe it would have been a very much fairer basis, because it would have got at what we want to get at, the excessive profits made during the war period. If manufacturers and other business men have not made excessive profits during the war period, they would not be called upon to pay. Under the minister's Bill, if they have ngt made more than 7 per cent they will not pay anything, but if they have made 5 per cent or 6 per cent, and they had not made profits to that extent for three years previously, according to my idea, they would have to pay a proportion of their profits as war taxation, and properly so.
As to the mining industry, I agree with the minister that the mining men throughout the country are perfectly willing to pay a war tax. I have yet to meet any class of people who are not willing to pay their fair .proportion. But my hon. friend takes too much on himself in this mining clause. He says it will be left to himself to estimate what the exhaustion of the mine is. He may know a great deal, and I think he does know a great deal about finance, but I do not think he knows anything about what is underneath the ground in a mine. The best mining engineers in Canada are very frequently mistaken as to the exhaustion of a mine. As far as I know, the principal objection of the mining men to the Bill as it stands is that the allowance of profit is not sufficient. A mine is supposed to earn more than 7 per cent and a mine is no good that does not earn more than 7; per cent at the same time exhausting its capital. A mine is no good if it does not earn 10 per cent while it is exhausting its capital. .The mining men say that the minister should have allowed a 10 per cent profit the same as to partnerships and individuals as well as making an allowance for the exhaustion of the mine. That is all I have to say about the mining provisions, because the minister has made up his mind to put this clause through.
It is wrong to call this a business profit tax. It should, in my opinion, be called a Bill to tax partial business profits because there are many manufacturers \tfho are not going to pay the tax. There are a great 
many manufacturers who are over-capitalized and would not come under the $50,000 capital proposal. Let me once more state that I do not believe any class of people in this country w-ant to evade fair taxation, but this is not going to be fair taxation. The man who has built up his business with untiring energy, who has put it on a profitable basis, who has kept his capitalization down to as low as $50,000 possibly is the man who is going to pay the tax. The man who has not put energy enough into his business to make it a profitable venture goes free, the man who has over-capitalized his business goes free while the man who ' has done his business legitimately, the man whom we want to encourage, who has worked night and day to build up his business is the man who will be paying the whole of this tax in so far as it is>
a tax on profits.

The hon. gentleman and
myself do not seem to understand the Bill alike. I understand that it is not capitalization but that it is the actual money that is invested in the business that they are allowed to earn 7 per cent on and that over-capitalization does not cut any figure.

We will see about that when it comes to he put into operation. It depends entirely on the interpretation of what capitalization is. The man who has kept his capitalization down is going to pay more than the man who has not done so. The man who has run his business on $50,000 capital, where he should have had a capital of $150,000,000 and is earning on that $50,000 12 or 15 per cent through his own energy and hard work, will have to pay more than the man who has got the same sized business with a capitalization of $150,000.
His reserve is considered as capital, and he will be allowed 7 per cent on that.

Yes, his reserve is shown by his statement, but a great many people's reserves are not shown by their statements. While very few people will try to evade their responsibility, this proposal puts a premium on evasion. Everybody who knows anything about manufacturing business knows that at the end of the year it entirely depends on the manufacturer's stocktaking methods as to his profits. The man who wants to evade the tax may do so. The minister will have a fine time making a valuation of a manufacturer's stock if he does not put in a proper state-

ment. The man. that puts in a proper statement will pay and the man who does not will not pay. I do not believe many will take advantage of that, but it is quite possible, and in many instances it is quite probable.' My hon. friend says that the collection of income tax would require the services of an army of officials. But it will take two armies to collect this unless the people are absolutely honest in their statements.
Is not the collection of an income tax subject to the same difficulties as those which my hon. friend has pointed out with regard to this method?
Not necessarily.
Persons make false statements as to their income.

They might put in false statements, but we know about their incomes in the towns. The assessors in the various towns and cities cannot be misled by a false statement of a man's income; it is known locally. I believe that my hon. friend could get his income tax. I am not advocating an income tax, hut I do not believe it would take the army of officers that he thinks it would. In ordinary towns his customs and inland revenue officers could easily get at the income of everybody in the place. They could do that without any difficulty and. it would give them something else to do besides playing golf in the afternoon, not that I object to those chaps playing golf.
They might overdo it.

Yes, but the ordinary taxpayer who is paying through the nose objects. I personally have no particular objection, but I think that my hon. friend could get at the income of people through the country to a viery great extent. As to the farmers, I agree with my hon. friend the minister that as farming is the basic industry of this country, it is well to- encourage it as far as possible. As far as I know the farmers are just as willing to pay their way and to pay what is necessary to bring this war to a successful conclusion as any other class of men in the community.

When I addressed the House on the resolution, I made certain overtures to the Minister of Finance regarding this proposed measure. I cannot quite concur with my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) in the view that there will be any difficulty in getting at the
capitalization of companies. I think that can be reached without very much difficulty.
I think it is an absolutely fair method which is proposed at the present time by this legislation. I wish to refer for a moment to what appear to me to be some anomalies in the Bill, and which I think are unfair to the country at large. The telegram that was read by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) to-<jay from the Rossland Board of Trade bears out my view, and is an evidence that the feeling of the people on our western coast is somewhat on the same line. The telegram in part reads as follows:
-and failing this, that the minimum capital affected be reduced to $25,000, and the spread between persons and corporations be changed from 3 to 2 per cent.
First of all, the minister has never yet given the House any reason, as far as I can recall, why the spread in Canada should be three per cent, when it is only one per cent in the United Kingdom. It has been explained that the rate was made six per cent for incorporated companies in the United Kingdom because money would not earn as much there, and seven per cent for individuals and partnerships . because they have not the advantages that incorporated stock holders enjoy. We are quite willing to accept that explanation as correct, but the minister has never yet explained why he made the spread in Canada three per cent instead of one per cent as in England. To illustrate, let us suppose there are two companies side by side, one an incorporated company and the other a . partnership, each with a capital of $400,000 and earning 10 per cent. The incorporated company will have to pay to the Treasury $3,000 per annum, and in three years it will have paid $9,000; whereas the partnership company, engaged in the same business and earning the same money, would not have paid one cent. To me that seems an anomaly.
With regard to the other recommendation of the Roseland Board of Trade, that the minimum be reduced to $25,000, I confess I think it a very wise suggestion, and in my judgment it would mean no greater cost for collection. The minister is taking power to ask the companies to have an accounting period, and those that have not had one in the past can be compelled to take stock and make a statement of their business to the minister. I repeat that I think it a wise suggestion to reduce the minimum capital to $25,000. For example, in a town of 5,000 people, an incorpor-

On section 1-short title:
What does the minister think about my suggestion of changing the title to "The Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When the Bill was under consideration I thought of inserting the word "War," but it occurred to me that it might be objectionable to call it a tax on war profits, as I suggested to my hon. friend this afternoon.
The worst of it is that it would not foe true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In some cases it might be undoubtedly a tax upon war profits, but in many cases- it would not be a tax upon war profits, at least direct war profits. In seme cases parties will pay this tax who have not derived their profits from the war directly or indirectly. Therefore I think it would be a mistake to call it a tax upon war profits.
Mr. A,. K. MACLEAN: No. I said: "The Business Profits War Tax Act." I think that is. different from "The Business War Profits Tax Act." We might let this section stand for the present.
Section stands.
On section 2-definitions:

In regard to the Board of Referees, I would like to have the minis-

ter'-s view. I hope the selection will not be made under the ordinary patronage system, nor that all the members of the board will be of one political stripe. I think the minister ought to say something about the policy that he will adopt in appointing the members of this board, as it is of great importance to the taxpayers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that I can answer my hon. friend except to say that it will be my abject to appoint men of good standing who will be absolutely fair in the discharge of their duties, which will be, in a sense, judicial. I do not know exactly what my, hon. friend means toy the ordinary patronage method of appointment. I certainly will endeavour to get good men for so responsible a position.

I think the minister understands what I mean, because it is well known that all the officials appointed by this Administration or by any party for that matter are usually of their own stripe; but in a matter of this kind, where both sides are equally interested and where there should be no political advantage giten to any one, it would be a very proper and fair thing if the minister should, in making his appointments, see that suitable men were selected and not confine himself to one political party.
There is another matter that I wish to draw to the attention of the minister-and perhaps this is as good a time as any- and that is the importance of publicity in regard to this assessment. I have not seen anything in the Bill which requires the minister to make public the assessment that he makes on those people who are liable to assessment. One of the great safeguards in the assessments that are made by the municipalities throughout Canada is the fact that they are published; that when the list is made out by the assessor 'of the city or the town, it is either published or placed in the office of the city or town, where every man can see it, and people know the business of their neighbours well enough to know whether thex assessment is fair or not. So far as I can judge, under this scheme the Department of Finance or the minister himself is the sole judge. He has abandoned the idea of taking the legal, well-known capital of a company as the basis; he has to fix that basis. All that work is thrown upon the minister. It is a very heavy task and he would be greatly assisted in
doing it properly by publicity. I would suggest to- him that he consider that point, and, if necessary, insert some clause in the Bill providing that the list of those whom he intends to tax in each province in Canada toe posted up so that all the people that are taxed may see how other people are taxed. In that way he will get a great deal of information that he cannot get in any other way. If he does not do that, the roan who lives across the street will not know what his neighbour is paying. He has a better idea than the minister has of what his neighbour is able to pay, and unless some publicity is given, it goes almost without saying that the taxation cannot be fairljl made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think it desirable that publicity should be given in the way that my hon. friend suggests. I have already said that, if Parliament desires a return, such a return . shall be brought down. This is a business tax dealing with private affairs of individuals, firms, and companies, engaged in business throughout the country, and while Parliament is entitled to any information as to the results of the tax, I do not believe the details should be advertised any more than is necessary.

It may be too late when Parliament is assembled for a man to get any advantage from the publicity, as the list is settled in September, and Parliament meets later on. It is not very much comfort to the man who has not received a fair show on the scheme of taxation to know that he can move in Parliament for a return and find out then what his neighbour has been taxed. I can see no objection to publicity. There is no objection under the municipal system and there should be none under the federal tax.

I quite agree with my hon. friend from Guysborough. All the information that he suggests the public should have is information that the public ought' to have. In order to have the fairness of any measure of taxation firmly established, it is necessary that everybody be sure that the tax is equitably imposed. So much discretion is left to the minister's department under this Act that he must concede that, putting it in the mildest way, there may be a lack of confidence in regard to the allotment of the taxation which could be avoided by publishing information as to the amounts paid under the

Act by different firms and corporations in the community.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The returns of assessment will be brought down to the House if asked for, as I have no doubt they will be asked for. Dominion taxation is different from provincial of municipal taxation. A great deal of discretion is necessarily reposed in the minister or his department, but that is true in the case of any taxing department; it is true with regard to the Customs Department and the Inland Revenue Department. Assessment will be made, there will be a right of appeal, the assessment will be fixed, the tax will follow and returns will be brought down by this Parliament. It .'feerns to me that in that way all necessary publicity is given.

I concur in what the minister has said. One reason why this information should not be published is the fact that of two companies in the same community one may have to pay and the other may not. To my mind it is very much better to keep that information in the department, and if any member of the House wants it he can get it in the regular way.

Do I understand the minister to say that no bluebook will be published containing the names of the firms taxed, the valuation of their properties, and the amount of their assessment under this Act? Will this information appear in any of the reports or publications of the department, or will it be kept privately in the minister's office, to be seen by no person except one who moves for a return in' Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My statement
is that returns will be brought down to the House of Commons if required by Parliament. I think it would be inadvisable to publish the returns in a bluebook or ,give details of the business of parties or firms assessed throughout Canada. Parliament, of course, is undoubtedly entitled to information as to the result of this tax a,nd as to the individuals or firms assessed under it. Take the Customs Department; details are not published in any bluebook, though the results are published.

speechtext:
Section agreed to. y

Will the minister tell us what (a) and (b) mean?
Sir THOMAS W'HITE:	My hon. friend
will recollect that under the Budget of 1915

a special War Revenue Act was brought down under which banks, trust and loan companies and insurance companies were specially taxed. They are liable to this Act, but the amount which they will pay under the special War Revenue Act will be deducted from the amount which they would otherwise be liable to pay under the provisions of this Act.

Suppose a company is
