Why is there a
difference between the tax imposed on an incorporated company and that which applies to a business owned by a firm or partnership?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry that my hon. friend was not present when this matter was under consideration by the committee, because we spent many hours in the discussion of that very question. I think it is generally conceded that if a man goes into business and risks his fortune in that business he' might' fairly receive 10 per cent upon the capital invested in the business as a return. On the other hand, 7 per cent is regarded as a
10 p.m. normal return upon the capital stock of a joint stock company. Further, an individual risks his entire fortune in his business, because' if he fails all his assets are liable for the business. On the other hand, in the case of a joint stock company a man limits his liability to the amount he puts into the company. For these and some other reasons that I could mention, but which it is probably not necessary for me to go into now, it was thought advisable to decide upon the 10 per cent rate in the case of individuals and the 7 per cent rate in the case of incorporated companies.

I asked the minister if he would not consider having a special clause providing for taxation on the turnover in the case of sales of war supplies, with a provision similar to that in the Bill with respect , to banks, by which hanks are exempted from payment of taxes under this Bill to the extent of the taxes imposed on them by the legislation of last year. I supported the minister a moment ago; perhaps he will support me now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will recall that I said that such a plan would work injustice in many cases, where

I
the profit on eales of war supplies is very small or where there is .no profit at all. The proposal, I think, would work hardship.	'
Mr. MeCREA: This measure is the most vicious piece of legislation ever put upon the Statute Book of any country, but we should endeavour to make the best of it and put it in the best shape possible. By subclause (a) the minister takes authority and power to decide all disputes, his de-. cision to be final and binding. We have not yet been told how he proposes handling the administration of the Act. This country is large. Does the minister propose to deal with this whole matter himself and to be the sole judge and umpire, or will it be handed over to a committee, or several committees? This may require quite a staff of officials, and'whilst I would have considerable confidence in the minister himself in dealing with these matters, and ' would accept his decision as final, I would not be prepared to thus accept the decisions of all the appointees he might make. My experience with officials appointed by the Government has been that they are sometimes very officious and sometimes annoying without cause. I have 'had some experience with appointees of the present Government in this respect, in my own particular business, where they spent a considerable time and caused some annoyance trying to make out a case when there was no case. I anticipate great cause for complaint, whether with reason or without reason, in the administration of the Bill. Where a corporation is supposed to be favourable to the Government, there may be a disposition not to look over their statement as. closely as those of political opponents of the Government. The Act would be bad enough if we were dealt with very leniently under it. I think this idea of the Government forcing themselves on the manufacturers as partners in their days, of prosperity, but having nothing to do with them ini their days of adversity, will not be found popular. In the last two or three years the manufacturers have made little or no profit. Just now there has been a turn in the tide, and many businesses are a little more prosperous, but when the war is over I doubt very much if that reign of prosperity will last very long. By this measure the Government proposes to be a partner with the manufacturers in our days of prosperity, but when days of adversity come they will
say: We have nothing to do with you now, you will stand alone or fall, just as you like. For my part I have absolutely no objection to paying and to being taxed my fair share in proportion for the funds necessary to carry on the war and the business of this country; but, as I have said before, I do not believe that'this tax will apply equitably. I said that it would not affect 50 per cent of the people of this country who are well able to pay. I say now it will not affect 20 per cent of the people in this position, but will affect some very injuriously and very unfairly. I rose to ask the minister to explain how he proposes to operate this measure so that we will have some measure of guarantee of how we are to be treated in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No measure of taxation will ever be popular, but, unfortunately, we have to resort to measures of taxation from time to time as the. public interest requires, and if ever there was a time in the history of Canada when special taxation was justifiable, I think it is now, in the midst of this war. I do not understand that my hon. friend in any way desires to avoid paying his fair share of taxation. Any taxation measure which has to be administered by the Dominion Government must be administered by some department. In this case the measure will be administered by the Department of Finance. The minister here means the minister, as head of the department, acting either by himself or through officials. It is not to be supposed that the minister will be able to give personal attention to every detail of the administration of a measure of this kind any more than it would be possible for the assessment commissioner of a city, who is generally responsible for the assessment of the city, to perform every act in connection with the assessment. But the minister is the responsible head of the department, and questions will be referred to him from time to time as they are in connection with all administrative duties of the department. We shall have to administer the Act from the department here; it will be necessary to have, a staff throughout the country, a certain number of officials who will assist, but assessments will be made from the Department of Finance here. We shall, in the first instance, call upon parties thought to be liable for a return. When, those returns come in they will be examined, and, if they are accepted, the assessments will be made accordingly.

If not, the assessment will be made according to the judgment of the department. In case of the party assessed feeling aggrieved, he has as his remedy an appeal to the board of referees, and if he is not satisfied with the judgment of the board of referees, then he has a further appeal to the Exchequer Court. In a general way, and only in a general way, that is what would happen under the administration of the Act.

I would call the attention of the Minister of Finance to the second clause of the Bill which states that " minister " means the Minister of Finance. I do not see how the minister can delegate his powers to his first clerk or second clerk or to any other assistant. Then in clauses 4 and 6 it says that the minister, that is, the Minister of Finance, shall determine what is to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will look up the Customs Act and other Act he will find that the minister is supposed to do everything. That means that the minister is responsible, acting for himself, or through his staff. I have administrative duties to perform every day. Sometimes I do them directly, and sometimes I consult with officials, but they are all done in the name of the minister. There are some sections of this Bill which require the exercise of the discretion of the minister himself. In these cases, the minister would exercise that discretion, but, so far as the making of the assessments throughout the country and the general administration of the Act are concerned, the intention is that they shall be done by the minister through hig staff.

I would like to have a statement from the minister in regard to a matter concerning which I have received, as, I think, other hon. gentlemen have received, communications. It is complained by the licensed fire insurance companies that, while they will be taxed, the fire insurance companies which are not licensed, and of which there is a large number in Canada, will escape. I do not exactly appreciate the distinction. I would 'like to know whether the minister has heard of the complaints, and what action will be taken with reference to them.

I think the situation,is,, that under the taxation Act of 1915, certain taxes -were imposed on fire insurance com-[Slr Thomas White.]
panies having licenses in Canada, while other companies, which do business without a license in Canada were not taxed. I think, that the point raised is by the insurance men who are interested in the licensed companies of Canada who object strongly that they should be taxed while companies that Are not licensed are not taxed under the Act of 1915.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is in this Bill too.

The point has been '
brought to my attention, as it seems to have been brought to that of my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and there has been a good deal of correspondence about it. I would like the minister to answer the question put by my hon. friend from Pictou, and tell us why those other companies are exempt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will realize that this Bill could not apply to unlicensed companies which are not carrying on business in Canada, because they could not be reached.

Why not?
Sir THOMAS-WHITE: Because they have no offices in Canada. The companies, to which reference is made, are companies like the New England mutuals, or other companies in the United States, or Lloyds, which have no offices in Canada, and which, therefore, can not be directly assessed in Canada. They do business in the Dominion in the way of insuring plants. The contracts' for such insurance can be made outside the boundaries of Canada, or an agent may come to Canada and write a policy. But the Dominion cannot impose a tax directly upon them because they are not represented here. That is recognized by the licensed insurance companies, but the suggestion was put forward that as we would not be able to reach those companies by reason of their not being domiciled in Canada, a tax should be imposed upon the premiums paid by business people in Canada who insure in such companies, so as to equalize matters. There is a good deal to be said for a tax of that kind, but I may point out that five or six years ago a Bill was introduced for that purpose in this Parliament, that it passed the House of Commons, but was rejected in the Senate. It was quite a controversial measure, and I do not believe that at this particular time it is desirable to introduce a Bill -which I think would give rise to a good deal of

controversy, that is, a Bill imposing taxation upon the premiums paid by business houses in Canada to those unlicensed companies. Personally I am of the view that, when the Insurance Act comes up for revision in this House, that question might properly be discussed, because there is a good deal to be said for the view of the licensed companies.
There is quite a large volume of business done by these New England companies, and it is quite unfair to the Canadian companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The mutual companies will not come under the provisions of this Act.
The fraternal societies are in the same position, are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I do not know whether I am right or not, but I do not see that the Bill specifies how often an accounting shall take place. Some of the best concerns in the country make their accounting twice a year, and if they took advantage of that they might make a profit of 14 per cent and not pay anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. If the
accounting period is for six months, the return will be made in respect to such accounting period. My hon. friend will observe from section 3 that the rate is 7 per cent per annum, so that the same principle will apply to the six months accounting periods.

Objection is raised by the licensed companies to the non-taxing of unlicensed companies. These unlicensed companies do a large amount of business in Canada amongst the manufacturers at a rate considerably lower than the licensed companies charge owing to certain conditions existing amongst themselves. I have had insurance agents come to me time and again last year about this very matter. I could not make out clearly why they were not taxed. I can see only one way of taxing the profits of these companies in Canada and that would be through the only people you could get at in Canada, namely, those who are paying the premiums. If these companies would allow those whom they insure a reduction equal to the amount of the tax they have to pay, I presume the manufacturers would not object to paying the tax. I see the difficulty which arises in taxing the premium directly. It might be done. I would urge the minister to consider it seriously, because, while by our tariff taxation and otherwise we are endeavouring to build up business in Canada, we seem to be putting a premium on companies that do not take out a license in Canada. I think the minister would be well advised if he would consider the matter very seriously and see if there is not some way of meeting this difficulty. Not only is there a very strong objection raised by the licensed companies themselves, but every representative they have in the Dominion is also deeply interested, as the minister can see, because these representatives do business largely on a commission basis and every premium they are deprived of not only injures the licensed company but really works detrimentally to the man in the field who solicits insurance.

I have brought this question up for a number of years. Whenever the minister has changed his tactics I have brought it up. At the time the present Insurance Act was up for consideration there was a great deal of discussion over this question. The manufacturers and the licensed insurance companies met before the Banking and Commerce Committee at that time, and after two or three weeks of discussion arrived at a solution. The insurance companies based their argument on the fact that the manufacturers were protected in everything they manufactured, while the insurance companies were not protected at all. While they employed large staffs, invested their money practically all in Canada, erected large buildings in cities and helped to build up the country to a very great extent, they were not protected at. all and there was no inducement for them to take out a license. Yet they took out licenses not only in the Dominion, but in every one of the provinces. They took up the question of what they called underground companies, the New England Mutual, the Reciprocal Underwriters, and the American, German and French Lloyds who do business in Canada without taking out any license whatever. The arrangement they came to in the Banking and Commerce Committee was that every assured person was to pay 15 per cent of the premium. The proposal was sent to the Senate, but the Senate struck out the clause''and put in a clause that the insured were to Teport to the Insurance Department the names of the underground companies that insured them and the amount of the premin ns. I think



they report that now. That is the way it .ended, but there has always been, a great deal of dissatisfaction on the part of licensed companies because they have to take out a license if they want to do business in an honest and straight-forward way. They carry all classes of business and the reciprocal underwriters only carry sprinkler risks. Recently the Board of Insurance Underwriters also started .a sprinkler department and they have a certain number of these risks themselves. At the same time they have to meet with an unfair competition. These unlicensed companies do not pay anything towards the upkeep of this country, they derive a profit from their business, or they would not do business, and that is why I have always urged upon the present Minister of Finance, as I urged upon the former Minister of Finance, that it was only reasonable and fair that these unlicensed companies should be forced to pay a certain .percentage on the premium which, of course, would have to be paid by the assured in this country. I think that ought to be included in this Bill.

I see that the minister has received a circular on this subject setting forth the arguments which are urged by the Insurance Federation in Canada in regard to the matter. They present the argument of the mutual companies that it would be inexpedient, having regard to the small amount involved, to impose taxation on these companies as it would involve a departure from the principle of the taxation of insurance companies directly. They suggest that the answer to this is that as a matter of general principle to impose a general tax upon one class of companies who are carrying on a legitimate fire insurance business and to permit another class to go free is a discrimination that is not fair. I think that the situation is on6 that should be dealt with from the war standpoint, apart from the general question which arose, and to which the minister alluded as having been dealt with toy special legislation some two years ago. I am at a lo-ss to understand why my hon. friend should exclude this class of people who are not licensed in this country, because the Bill provides that foreign companies doing the business in Canada on other lines shall contribute. I did not see any reason why, in dealing with foreign companies doing business in Canada, my hon. friend does not tax these

unlicensed companies in the same way that he taxes other foreign companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These insurance companies have no offices in Canada. I do not know that it is urged at all that we could reach them directly. It is suggested that by reason of the fact of not being able to reach them directly the tax should be levied on the premium paid by the insured in Canada.

In a great many cases these companies do not have offices in Canada, but it is well recognized that these risks can be placed. The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has put the point. We all know where they are. They are really doing business here. The contractors may toe in New York, or some other place, but they really insure the manufacturer here against loss by fire just as effectively as any company in Canada could.
It is suggested in this memorandum that those who place insurance with unlicensed companies should be compelled to make returns to the Superintendent of Insurance; and that those returns should be 'accompanied by a statement covering the percentage decided upon; and that it should be incumbent upon any one recovering a loss from the company to prove that the taxes and premium had been paid. Those are the methods which are suggested by the licensed companies for dealing with this matter. It does seem anomalous that under our system unlicensed companies who take blanket risks in a great many ways should be able to do business free from all the restrictions that apply to licensed companies. I am sure the minister appreciates the argument which has been made in favour of taxing these unlicensed companies if they can be taxed, but I understood him to say that the expense involved in collection would do away with whatever money might be derived. I think a tremendous amount of insurance of that kind is being done in Canada, and I should like to know on what ground the minister justifies his not attempting to make these people pay under this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would not be possible to do that under this Bill, because we cannot tax directly an insurance company carrying on business in New England, for instance, and having no office in Canada. I do not think it would toe within the power of the Dominion Government to impose a direct tax upon a non-Canadian

company having no place of business in Canada.	'
You cou'ld tax the contract.	,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But that would not come under the provisions of this Act. In order to do that we should have to have a supplementary measure of taxation. It might be- done, let us say, by an amendment to the Insurance Act, but it could not be done under this measure. Not only that, but as most of these are mutual companies their earnings would not make them liable under the provisions of this. Act. My own view is that there is a great deal to be said for the contention of the insurance people, and when the Insurance Act is under revision again this question will have to be considered and dealt with. My predecessor had a great deal of difficulty with it. I am told that there was no question that was more discussed at the session of 1910, deputations coming from various parts of Canada representing business interests. We are imposing a -tax upon the business people of Canada under this Bill. It is now suggested that we should impose a further tax, and tax the premiums which people pay to- these insurance companies. I think that would be a highly controversial question, and., considering the experiences in this House and the Senate in 1910, I do not think it would be advisable to consider such a tax at the present time.
In 1910, fifteen per cent was suggested before the committee as a compromise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Am { not right in saying that it was a highly controversial question ?
It undoubtedly was. .

I understand the minister's attitude, although I can see no reason why a supplementary measure to reach these people should not be introduced. Will not the mutual insurance companies incorporated, under provincial charter, and doing ibusines-s in that way, be .reached by this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they make the stipulated profits they are liable, notwithstanding that they are provincial incorporations, but I think the companies my hon. friend has in mind would hardly make the profits to render them liable.

Subsection (b) of clause 3 reads:
166* [DOT]
(b) That the dividends received from the stock of any incorporated company which has paid a tax upon its profits under the provisions of this Act shall not be included when the profits of any business are -being determined.
That I suppose is to protect a holding company which holds the stock of an incorporated company. I would suggest that it is possible for a holding company to hold shares or an interest in an unincorporated concern. I have known such cases myself, and in order that companies holding an interest in an unincorporated company should not be doubly taxed, I think we should add something to this sub-section, and I would suggest the words " or any shares or interest in an unincorporated company."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have gone
pretty far in exempting the holding company in respect of dividends derived from companies whose stock they hold. The income tax of the United States applies to all holding companies in respect of their entire profits. I am not quite sure that 1 understand my hon. friend.

He says that you are exempting the profits which one incorporated company holds in another, but making no exemption when the holding company has an interest in a firm or partnership. For instance, a shipping company might own 32-64ths of a ship, which is practically a partnership.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought we
had gone pretty far with regard to holding companies, but I will consider that suggestion. We can let the subsection stand.

How would the minister
deal with a case of this kind? Stocks, oi course, of every kind are higher than they were twelve months ago, 10 per cent increase being about the average; that is, a man who takes an inventory in 1915 would probably find his goods were worth in per cent more than they were worth in 1914. The minister, I presume, would consider that as part of the profits of the year. But how would he deal with it' when it comes to the last accounting period in 1917? Before the man has got rid of his stock, it may have dropped in value. It is certainly likely to drop after the war. What would the minister do in that case? VVould he reap the benefit of the increased value of the inventory in 1916 over 1915, and allow the owner to stand the loss if the value of the -stock decreased in 1917?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would depend upon the value at the time of the stock-

taking for the accounting period. So far as capital is concerned, that will be determined as from the beginning of the accounting period. The value of the stock would be taken and the accounts made up at the end of the accounting period.
I mean the stock on hand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Stock on hand
and the accounts as made up would show the profits for the accounting period. I do not think we can assume that the price is going to drop at a certain time; if you assume that, you cannot make your assessment at all. You have to deal with your stock for the accounting period on its merits.
Mr. MoORAE: The price of shells might drop a great deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Of course, it
would not be good business to take the stock at its full value. You might be justified in having a contingent account to take care of any drop that might occur. No rule can be laid down as to that; it is a question of fact in each case of what are the true profits for each accounting period.
I am just asking for information to know how the minister intends to deal with such matters.

As I understand it, the
general rule in taking stock is to take stock at cost price, and if it be worth more money at that time, that is an anticipated profit that goes into next year's business.
If the stock depreciates, what do you do?

You reduce the amount if it depreciates. I think that is the custom of the trade. If the stock has depreciated in value, you put it down at its proper value at the time the stock is taken, and the proper value in no case is greater than the cost price.

Will subsection
(b) stand?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not see my way to agree to that unless some concrete case is brought to my attention.

I can hardly see how
you can logically exclude such dividends. There would be ho harm in letting the subsection stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All right.

Is there any variation
from the resolution in the first eight sections of the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No.
Subsection (b) stands.
Section 3, with the exception of subsection (b), agreed to.
On section 4-accounting period defined.

I presume that, if a firm is in the habit of taking stock at the end of six months just to see how its business is panning out, but still carries it forward to the end of the year, the annual statement will be all that is necessary for the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is all that is necessary.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 5-trades and businesses included :

During the discussion of
this section when the resolution was before the House, I made the following statement as reported in Hansard, page 2054:
Mr. Loggie: I wish to bring a case to the attention of the Minister of Finance, and ask him how he could possibly arrange a basis for taxation in that case. Take, for example, the Arm X referred to, that of Armstrong & Ferguson. This firm had an order to supply the army, if you like, with certain commodities. In the tourse of three months they sold $3,000 or $4,000 worth. So far as any record shows, the Arm was not in existence before that time, and it went out of business three or four months later, and was succeeded by William Ferguson, who, I believe, is the Ferguson of the firm.
I want to say here that I was not right when I made the statement so far as any record showed the firm was not in existence before that time. I have reason to believe that the firm was in business for pearly i year before war was declared; that it continued for three months thereafter; that it executed contracts during the three months, but that the contract was not completed, and that William Ferguson, who is the Ferguson of the firm of Armstrong and Ferguson, succeeded to the business. I think it only fair that l should make this correction. I was making an illustration of this firm, showing the minister the difficulties I saw in the way of his enforcing subsection a of section 5; but, of course, the circumstances are somewhat changed, and it is very much as the minister said in his reply: it depends on the facts. When the facts were found out,

if the capital was in the business and the profits were made, provided that the war supplies were not less than 20 per cent of the business, then there would be a tax; but if the war supplies were less than 20 per cent of the turnover of the business, then there would not be any tax on the war supplies even although the firm earned a very large profit. It seems to me that section 5 will be difficult to operate, because it will be hard to get at the facts as to what portion of war supplies we are to expect some tax from. The minister, however, in his reply to me, said it was a matter of fact; that the question was a matter of capital and earnings, and what were the total sales of the firm and the total sales of war supplies. The members of this firm are still at Newcastle; and if they are liable for a tax under the law, I think they will be perfectly good for it, although the firm was dissolved about three months after war was declared.	-

When the resolutions were before the House, an hon. member opposite from the province of Ontario stated that there were quite a large number of companies incorporated in that province with a capital of $40,000 for the purpose of evading some local tax or for some other reason. He stated that they were doing well, many of them making money; that many of them would wish to come under the operation of this measure, and that a considerable sum of money could be obtained in that way. Is there anything in that statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thinik I can say that no petitions have been received from such companies asking to be brought under t'he provisions of the Act. If the minimum amount of capitalization were reduced to $40,000 it would be urged that companies with a capitalization of $30,000 ought to be included. If they have a capital of $50,000, they will be liable; if they have a capital of less than $50,000, they will not be liable. With Tegard to the title of this Bill, referred by the hon. member for Halifax I would move that [DOT]section 1 be amended by inserting the word "war" before the word "tax" in the first line thereof.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As to subsection (b) of section 31, a question was raised by the hon. member for Guysborough and by the hon. member for Halifax. The wording of that subsection is:
That the dividends received from the stock of any incoroprated company which has paid a tax upon its profits under the provisions of this Act shall not be included when the profits of any business are being determined.
I do not quite understand what amendment is suggested. Hon. gentlemen will observe that the words used are "the dividends received from the stock of any incorporated company."

What was meant was this: If company "A" incorporated holds Shares in company "B" incorporated, and company "B" has paid the war tax under the provisions of this Bill, that fact should be taken into consideration in determining the assessment of company "A" incorporated. Supposing company "A" incorporated holds a half interest in a partnership carrying on a business similar to that carried on by the incorporated company, and supposing that partnership has assets in excess of $50,000 and has paid the tax; should that not be taken into consideration whehi assessing the taxation payable by company "A" incorporated? The cases are exactly the same except that the company in which the incorporated company "A" holds an interest is in the one case another incorporated company while in the other case it is a partnership.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would my hon. friend think that the word "dividends" would, be apt in both cases? That is what I am not clear upon.
I think the minister would have to recast the whole 'section in order to cover the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will let it stand until we have a chance to consider it.

If a corporation
which had been in existence for some years and which had a capitalization of $40,000 at a time later than the coming into force of this Act increased its capitalization to $50,000, would this Act apply to that company only from the date upon which the formal increase of capitalization was effected?
Sir THOMAS WH1,TE: Subsection a of section 5 says:
The business of any person the capital employed in which has been throughout the accounting period less than fifty thousand dollars.
The word, "throughout" is used.

As a matter of legal interpretation, unless the word "eontinu-

ously" was used, the word "throughout" might not be held to>
cover the whole period.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is an exception which only applies if the capitalization has been less than $50,000 throughout the accounting period.

Supposing only last October a company had increased its capitalization to over $50,000, would the minister toe able to go hack to the accounting period previous to January 1, 1915, the first accounting period, and make the tax payable from that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If during an accounting period a company increased its capital front $40,000 to $50,000, it would be liable in respect of that accounting period in respect of the capital employed during that accounting period.
Section 5 agreed to.
Progress reported.
